items.body: Shell and Core takes its title from the unfinished concrete structures that have become fixtures of the Syrian landscape, and Tasgeelat Al-Husni تسجيلات الحُسني uses that image of arrested construction as a way of looking at lives left incomplete. Much of the record is assembled from things heard or observed in everyday life: bureaucratic rituals, checkpoints, cars, street conversations, scrap collectors and an uncle’s absurd political opinions. On “Spacetune” these details accumulate into a comic story that deliberately goes nowhere; “Existing” turns repetition and waiting into its subject, while the heavier “Grinder” pushes familiar material towards something more grotesque. The humour is important. Rather than presenting Syria exclusively through catastrophe, Tasgeelat Al-Husni draws on a local tradition of satire and everyday mockery in which absurdity is one means of living with circumstances that have themselves become absurd. The music operates in much the same way, refusing a clean division between local tradition and experimental electronics. The oud can introduce the relatively spacious “Existing”, sit behind electronic and guitar noise on “Spacetune”, or grind against doom-laden riffs on “Grinder”. Al-Husni explicitly rejects using the instrument as a nostalgic signifier of a disappearing culture; here it belongs to the present as naturally as synthesis, distortion or field recording. Progressive and heavy rock are equally embedded in the record’s vocabulary, particularly in its abrupt shifts between calm and physical weight. Lazar Mečanin’s production makes those contrasts unusually pronounced: passages of relative openness can suddenly thicken into distortion, low-frequency pressure and noise, giving the album the unstable logic of the environment it describes. One of the album’s most striking changes of register comes on “Perspective”, where the voice of Ukrainian opera singer Oksana Vakula introduces a radiant tone, briefly opening up the record’s otherwise rough and unstable sonic terrain. That makes the unfinished Massar Discovery Center on the cover more than an illustration. Along with Syria’s other abandoned concrete shells, it becomes an architectural counterpart to a record about interrupted trajectories. Yet Shell and Core avoids turning incompletion into a grand metaphor. What matters most is the peripheral and the discarded: things overheard, jokes, irritating routines, incongruous sounds and surreal encounters. The picture of Syria that emerges is at the same time damaged and precarious, but also mundane and funny, a place whose exposed structural bones are filled with everyday life. To help us better understand the production process for Shell and Core we reached out directly to Tasgeelat Al-Husni. Throughout عَ العَضم (Shell and Core), everyday Syrian life is depicted in a way that often feels almost surreal, allowing the ordinary and the mythical to coexist. The repeated “unknown” in “Spacetune”, the taxi driver nicknamed Azrael—the Angel of Death—blasting heavy dabke, the endless bureaucracy of “Existing”, the Ladas, and finally the litany of scrap collectors all feel like fragments of the same social landscape. There is also a distinctly sardonic humour running through the writing. Do you think of your lyrics as poetry, documentary montage, social commentary or simply another way of composing with sound? Most of the lyrics are rephrasing of something I have heard in Syria either in a conversation with friends or randomly on the street. I wrote down some of what I had heard and then integrated them with how I thought of each song. I am new to writing words, so I don’t know much, but I have tried writing a comical story with mild suspense that leads nowhere on “Spacetune,” describing recurrent scenes from daily life on “Existing,” and creating some surreal visual scenes on “Grinder.” The sardonic humor is essential to the environment where the album came from. It’s in the music we hear (such as the music of the Rahbani family), the TV we watch (such as Spotlight – بقعة ضوء), the books we read (such as Muhammad al-Maghut’s), so you would also hear it in your day-to-day life from your relatives, your college friends, the bus driver or even from a soldier on a checkpoint. Add to that the absurdity of people’s takes on the conflict, like that uncle on Spacetune, which naturally calls for mockery. Peugeot 504 – photo by Hussain Hussain The second track, “Existing”, opens with an oud before gradually expanding into a much broader electronic landscape. The instrument never feels nostalgic or symbolic of tradition; instead, it becomes another texture within the composition. Was it important for you to avoid treating the oud as a marker of cultural identity, allowing it instead to coexist naturally with electronics and noise? It was! I think such instruments are not supposed to sound like a distant cry from the past echoing in an empty space, or “a ghostly remnant from a lost culture”, like David Byrne once wrote. The oud, like any instrument, should be used to serve the song the way the song is meant to be. It definitely could be used in its classical character with takasim and as accompaniment for singing like on “Existing,” but it can also accompany heavy doom metal riffs to add a bloody drilling texture on “Grinder,” or do some finger picking behind synth and guitar noises like on Spacetune. If you listen to a based folk performance from the past, you hear the oud vital and integrated with the rest of the instruments, not sounding like an anomaly, and I think this is how it should be treated in any other (modern) context. Window – photo by Hussain Hussain Although the album is rooted in electroacoustic composition and experimental electronics, there are moments—particularly in the treatment of distortion, low-frequency weight and rhythmic pressure—that recall progressive rock, heavy rock and noise. Are those traditions part of your musical vocabulary, and how do they intersect with the experimental and electronic music you make today? These traditions strongly influence how we have approached this record and music making in general. The treatment of sound at this level was more Lazar’s part, so I have forwarded the question to him, and this is his response: “Those traditions have to be a part of our vocabulary given the fact it’s the music we grew up on – Floyd, Crimson, etc. These bands influenced us as players but they also influenced how we think about music. A song can exhibit cinematic properties and sometimes be even more immersive than a movie if done right. The record is really a landscape representing every-day life in Syria (if I understood it correctly myself hah), moments of beauty and calmness intertwined with unpredictable chaos mostly right next to each other, so in a way the music is interpreting life, and by using these acoustic and production techniques we are attempting to recreate the feelings one might have simply living there.” Random Structure – photo by Hussain Hussain How do you see your work in relation to other Syrian experimental musicians? Is there a shared aesthetic or set of concerns emerging from the scene, or do you feel that each artist is responding to the experiences of recent years in fundamentally different ways? I have learned a lot from contemporary Syrian and Arab artists — Tootard, Shabjdeed, Khaled Allaf, Lynn Adib, Al-Rahel Al-Kabir, Kulna Sawa, and many more — and that has encouraged me to work on my own stuff, sing about what I have heard or seen, and eventually release that. It is true that everyone is responding to their experiences in their own way; some express that in a desperate way, some in a cynical way, some tackle social issues, and some speak about personal experiences. Maybe what we have in common is our frustration and disgust with our situation now and in recent years, but who knows? What’s important to me is that many of our artists sound so fresh, so unique and so relevant, and I always look forward to hearing their new approaches and what they are talking about. The cover features the unfinished Massar Discovery Center (“Massar Rose”) in Damascus—a project that was meant to embody education, innovation and the future before construction stopped in 2014. Throughout the album, there is a recurring sense of lives shaped by interruption: bureaucratic waiting, checkpoints, abandoned trajectories and systems that never quite reach completion. Did you see the building as encapsulating that condition, or were you drawn to it for different reasons? Gardenia Towers – photo by Hussain Hussain Exactly, hence the name, ع العضم Shell and Core! The rest of the album art (partly prepared for a CD release) features some well-known incomplete buildings, such as the infamous 50-year-old Yalbugha Tower in the middle of the capital and the Gardenia Towers in Homs that became known among the public as the “Death Towers”, used by snipers during the war. Such giant incomplete, mostly ugly, structures are so common to see in Syria. They are ironically reflective of the life of Syrian individual that has become so crippled, it might never reach a sense of completion. Everyone who lost their home forever and had to live in a tent, everyone that lost their beloved ones, got detained for the stupidest reason, or had to serve in the army for 8 years or so, and also everyone who just had to live or grow up there during these awful times. To me, this building not only encapsulates these incomplete trajectories, but also resembles, with its bare bones (عضم) sticking out, how naked, exposed and fragile we are. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以叙利亚未完工的建筑意象切入，将官僚仪式、检查站、街头对话等日常声响作为素材，构筑出一种荒诞而日常的生活图景。音乐拒绝将乌德琴简单地作为文化怀旧符号，而是与合成器、失真、田野录音自然共存，形成本地传统与实验电子的开放对话。制作上突出了平静与压迫之间的突然切换，低频与噪音时常从空旷段落中骤然涌出，营造出与所描述的环境一致的逻辑。乌克兰歌剧人声的加入在粗粝的声景中短暂开辟出明亮空间，与封面的废弃建筑形成互文。整体回避了将叙利亚仅作为灾难呈现的视角，转而通过嘲讽与荒诞来描绘一个受损却依然在日常运转的地方。

items.excerpt: John Coltrane - One Down, One Up: Live At the Half Note (recorded 1965, released 2005), My Favorite Things: Coltrane At Newport (recorded 1963 and 1965, released 2007), Offering: Live At Temple University (recorded 1966, released 2014), A Love Supreme: Live In Seattle (recorded 1965, released 2021), Evenings At the Village Gate: John Coltrane with Eric Dolphy (recorded 1961, released 2023) By Lee Rice Epstein 1965 was remarkably transformative year in Coltrane’s history. items.body: John Coltrane - One Down, One Up: Live At the Half Note (recorded 1965, released 2005), My Favorite Things: Coltrane At Newport (recorded 1963 and 1965, released 2007), Offering: Live At Temple University (recorded 1966, released 2014), A Love Supreme: Live In Seattle (recorded 1965, released 2021), Evenings At the Village Gate: John Coltrane with Eric Dolphy (recorded 1961, released 2023) By Lee Rice Epstein 1965 was remarkably transformative year in Coltrane’s history. Thankfully, through its ongoing archival releases, Impulse Records has continued to fill in the picture of how, as an artist, he continually pushed himself and his band, deeply and passionately giving his all at all times. One Down, One Up takes us right to March 26, 1965, where Coltrane, McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones play an astonishingly high-wire, high-energy “One Down, One Up” that runs nearly 30 minutes. The electricity crackling between players says exactly why Coltrane still matters, why he’s still adored, and why countless players of all kinds continue to study and revere him. The set’s recapitulation on the Newport stage months later (the second half of My Favorite Things: Coltrane At Newport ), more clearly shows how the group was thinking about and working through their headiest ideas. That the Newport set was released with a 1963 performance featuring Roy Haynes in the drummer seat gives some additional dimensions to the quartet’s changes over time. Tyner and Jones moved on by the next year, while Garrison held down the Alice Coltrane, Rashied Ali, and Pharoah Sanders group. Reportedly, he didn’t play with them in the fall of 1966, when Coltrane led a phenomenal set at Temple University. Offering has been alternately reviled and lauded, cited by some as a polished but unnecessary bootleg for completists only. But, if one just takes a step back and considers Offering happening the same season as Albert Ayler’s seminal European tour—with the quintet of Ayler, Donald Ayler, Michel Samson, Bill Folwell, and Beaver Harris—and if one wants to get really interested in sympathetic wavelengths, you hear Coltrane singing reportedly for the first time ever during “Leo” on November 11, 1966, while Ayler was recorded doing the same on a performance of Sanders’s “Japan” the previous night, November 10, 1966. That Ayler later screamed during his memorial performance for Coltrane would be too on the nose if someone manufactured it. The two shared both intellectual and spiritual bonds, a beautiful thing we’re scarcely able to know of or understand even partly. As the saying goes, it would have been enough to get these first three albums, but the 2020s has produced two seemingly impossible sessions: a live recording of “A Love Supreme,” also from 1965, and an unissued session with Eric Dolphy from 1961, featuring “Greensleeves” and “Africa.” What, truly can be said about Coltrane and Dolphy that doesn’t lead to a mountain of what-if or if-only hypotheticals? The hour-plus set is fiery and rich with ideas in motion. If someone told me this was 1963 or ’64, I wouldn’t doubt it. By ’61, both Coltrane and Dolphy were already well out in front of many contemporaries, and the mutual support demonstrated during their brief time together is beautifully realized here. On A Love Supreme (fascinatingly, recorded a couple days after Live In Seattle), Coltrane leads a kind of crossover group, with Tyner, Garrison, and Jones as the core quartet, joined on the tour by Sanders and Donald Garrett on bass, with Carlos Ward jumping in on sax at Coltrane’s invitation. Both Coltrane and Sanders add percussion along with Jones’s drumming, and if Offering represents some kind of approaching end point in Coltrane’s art, the Seattle performance of “A Love Supreme” leads in the same direction, ever forward. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评聚焦Impulse唱片公司为纪念Coltrane诞辰一百周年而梳理的一系列档案录音，时间跨度从1961年与Dolphy的合作到1966年Temple大学的现场，涵盖了他音乐生涯最具变革性的时期。评论详细追溯了Coltrane四重奏到后期五重奏的演变，以及1965年经典四重奏与1966年新阵容之间的过渡。通过将Coltrane在Temple大学的演出与Albert Ayler同期的欧洲巡演并列审视，揭示了两位先锋之间深刻的精神共鸣与即兴理念的呼应。文章还讨论了Offering这张被部分乐迷视为多余bootleg的专辑如何在新语境下重新获得意义，以及Dolphy早逝所带来的无尽假设。评论展现出对自由即兴、前卫精神与历史语境的高度洞察。

items.album: Patriarchy Stage a Tableau of Floral Worship in Video for “Lilylicker”
items.excerpt: Tear a piece of this and shove it hard into your mouth A lilylicker sounds like a particularly devoted suck-up, someone whose admiration has become a full-time occupation. items.body: Tear a piece of this and shove it hard into your mouth A lilylicker sounds like a particularly devoted suck-up, someone whose admiration has become a full-time occupation. Put the word beside Oscar Wilde’s fascination with actresses Lillie Langtry and Sarah Bernhardt, and a whole society of worshippers comes into view: flowers, flattery, beautiful women placed upon pedestals. Wilde was a cunning linguist, of course, though Patriarchy have a few suggestions about putting that talent to more practical use. The lily remains a lovely flower, of course, though its innocence becomes somewhat harder to maintain once somebody starts licking it. The Los Angeles snuff-pop duo of Actually Huizenga and AJ English, otherwise known as The Drummer, premieres the video for Lilylicker, taken from their new EP, Appendices. Written and produced by Huizenga and English, the song takes its initial inspiration from Wilde’s devotion to those celebrated performers, then puts the woman receiving all that attention in charge of the proceedings. A menacing bass synth and a blunt kick drum set the terms, leaving Actually’s near-whispered vocal close enough to feel conspiratorial. Her poetic purr slips between the beats before the track opens into a metallic industrial-techno rhythm, bringing the hard physicality of ’90s industrial into contact with contemporary darkwave. The bass keeps its grip while crushed guitars tear through the chorus, making the move from intimate persuasion to open command feel deliciously abrupt. The words play a similar game. Wanting to be liked becomes wanting to be licked; affection, appetite, and obedience get tangled in the same exchange. Actually moves from seeking approval to prescribing exactly how it should be delivered, with an impatience that gives the song its humor. For all the literary ancestry, the central proposition is straightforward: admiration should have practical applications. Directed by Patriarchy and shot by Hazel Hill McCarthy, the video makes that business of putting people on pedestals unusually literal. Figures revolve on small platforms against an almost uninterrupted black background, their costumes and gestures exposed by direct light. Actually appears in a white gown holding lilies, in a pale pink dress draped with chains, and in a metallic corset with enormous gold wings and a guitar. English handles a skull while wearing little white wings; their young son appears in family tableaux and as a cherub perched on a classical column. The arrangements suggest devotional statues brought to life by people with their own ideas about sainthood. There is an affectionate absurdity to these living ornaments. The solemn poses give way to movement, expressions change, and the family portrait keeps interrupting the fantasy of immaculate statuary. Against all that black space, the slightest human detail becomes conspicuous. Even the insects have supporting roles. The setting came about through necessity. According to the band, the owner of their original studio location objected to the proposed content and the presence of their son, who was also appearing in the video. With the shoot abruptly displaced, the crew relocated to the Angeles woods and rethought the production outdoors. Huizenga subsequently edited the footage “happily alone and for many hours,” describing editing as “one of my secret pleasures.” “I decided not to retouch anything either. So all razor bumps, dark circles, cellulite, and sock lines are fully visible if you wish to judge me physically… I had a baby, so kill me! The boys are perfect though. A lot of the things that went ‘wrong’ ultimately added to the beauty of it, like having to shoot outside, where moths kept flying in front of our lenses, drawn in by the bright lights” For Huizenga, leaving those imperfections intact also connects to Patriarchy’s larger, apocalyptic view of power: “Patriarchy has never been about perfection, it’s about realizing we are the last remnants of human existence before AI enslaves us all; that’s why the project is called Patriarchy after all, patriarchy is the final human ruling order. Our next masters wont be women or men or human in any form, so we need to embrace our chaos and imperfections while we can.” Watch the video for Lilylicker below: Released in the wilting days of this past Summer, Appendices brings together five songs developed across different periods of the band’s life, reaching back to The Unself sessions and forward through the aftermath of 2025’s Manual For Dying. These recordings have survived abandoned versions, rewrites, and changes substantial enough to turn industrial tracks into orchestral ballads and minimal synth into metal. Alongside Lilylicker, the EP includes Bite Marks, Servile, Ode (to an Apprehensive Tyrant), and Hate Fuck, with additional production and mixing contributions across the record from Ben Chisolm and Matia Simovich. Huizenga’s reading supplies another connection between these otherwise unruly songs. Wilde, Marchesa Luisa Casati, Emperor Tiberius, and the Manson family furnish starting points for examinations of sexuality, submission, obsession, and violence. Across three full-length albums, a live record, and numerous remixes, Patriarchy have pursued those interests through industrial electronics, synth-pop, metal, and performance art. Appendices also documents Huizenga and English becoming an increasingly self-contained production team, with Lilylicker pointing toward the club without surrendering their taste for theatrical excess. That appetite for the personal and the unruly carries into Actually’s Sex and the Pity, Huizenga’s new podcast and livestream concept, whose pilot is announced for this Friday at 10 p.m. Pacific. Pitched as Elvira meeting Gore Vidal, it promises secret guests, fireside conversation, and previously untold stories from Patriarchy’s tours and beyond, forming a living journal for a future film project. “I can only really seem to recount these hilarious stories properly when I’m talking one-on-one with a cute gay at a party; so I’m gonna try to recreate that free-form energy for the podcast.” Listen to Lilylicker below and order the Appendices EP here. items._cn_summary: 这张作品以王尔德对女演员的崇拜为灵感起点，将文学典故转化为音乐叙事。低沉的贝斯合成器与钝感的底鼓奠定压迫基调，歌手近乎耳语的声线在节拍间穿梭，随后展开为金属质感的工业-techno节奏，将九十年代工业的硬朗物理感与当代暗潮融合。歌词将渴望被喜欢转化为被舔舐的隐喻，亲密劝诱与公开命令之间的转换制造出突兀张力。MV由乐队自导，黑底布景中人物在小平台上旋转，白裙、粉裙、金属胸衣搭配金色翅膀与吉他，家庭成员共同构建活人雕塑式的宗教画。声音设计层次分明，工业节拍与碾核吉他交织，形成文学性与身体感兼备的暗潮文本。

items.body: Label: Burning Ambulance Records, 2026 Personnel - Wadada Leo Smith: trumpet; Sylvie Courvoisier: piano (#1,3); Marcus Gilmore: drums (#1,3); Bobby Naughton: vibraphone (#2-5); Lamar Smith: electric guitar (#2,3,5); Bill Laswell: electric bass (#3,4); Melvin Gibbs: electric bass (#3,4); Mauro Refosco: percussion (#2,3,5); Brian Jawara Gray: percussion (#2,3,5); Pheeroan akLaff: drums (#2-5). Trumpeter and composer Wadada Leo Smith assembled various ensembles for his new album, Constellations and Hemispheres , rooted in harmonic intensity, open structures, and modal depth. The project was sparked by quantum physics, parallel universes, and shifting dimensions, in a no-nonsense approach that explores timbre and atmosphere with serious intentions and exceptional versatility. The album kicks off in trio format, with Smith joining forces with the quick-witted pianist Sylvie Courvoisier and adaptable drummer Marcus Gilmore on “ Dark Energy ”. Cymbal activity is paired with sparse piano texture, while Smith's declamations extend from sharply piercing to dolefully lugubrious. This mournful reflection swells and intensifies via Courvoisier's phenomenal work, expanding and contracting by way of intricately coiling patterns that work as a perfect foil for Smith's obscure idioms. Gilmore is granted a brief unaccompanied passage. " Lake Tanganyika " emerged from a sextet session with trumpet, vibraphone, guitar, percussion, and drums. Ancient, water-surrounded landscapes are evoked via the emotionally powerful lyricism brought by Smith over Bobby Naughton's gossamer vibes and Pheeroan AkLaff's gloriously relentless drum flow. The seasoned drummer also gets our attention on the closer, " Meditation on Love ", a cosmic, open-ended manifesto of peace and hope. Smith traces a spiritual and artistic connection with the Rastafari—associated with the reggae music of Jamaica—but I'm unable to spot that influence here. Yet the music is able to knife through the speakers like a lightning bolt. " Dark Matters, Particles of Light, Mirror of the Unseen " is a full-length workout clocking in at 22 minutes. Powerful and moody, the piece is bookended by the same trio that had shaped the opening track, expanding in its middle part into an octet featuring two distinguished electric bassists, Bill Laswell and Melvin Gibbs, who contribute to the dismal, apocalyptic scenario with authority. A lighter, tactile percussive quality appears by the end, relieving the pressure. The two bassists are also prominent on " Deep Canyons on Mars ", diffusing ominous vibes through gravelly distorted sounds. The heavy, nightmarish tones are pacified when vibraphone and trumpet step forward, yet obscurity still lives here when the bass returns with wah-wah bluesy sounds drowned in electronics. Though the result of multiple sessions, Constellations and Hemispheres feels like a unified experiment—mostly stripped down of gloss but still with haunting and transcendent moments to reflect upon. Favorite Tracks: 01 - Dark Energy ► 02 - Lake Tanganyika ► 03 - Dark Matters, Particles of Light, Mirror of the Unseen
items._cn_summary: Wadada Leo Smith 的《Constellations and Hemispheres》以量子物理与平行宇宙为概念框架，将多组不同编制的小型合奏交织成一张统一但层次分明的专辑。作品围绕和声张力、开放结构与调式纵深展开，开篇三曲以钢琴-鼓-小号为核心，呈现稀疏织体与尖锐抒情之间的剧烈切换；中段加入电吉他、颤音琴与打击乐，唤起古老水域般的冥想氛围。一段二十二分钟的群奏以两组电贝斯共同构建末日般的低频场景，最终以轻盈的打击乐质感释放压力。全作去除了修饰性光泽，却在留白与轰鸣之间保留可反复聆听的精神性。小厂牌发行，原创乐评质量扎实，与实验爵士及前卫即兴偏好高度契合。

items.body: Thematically, Post Dub Cities hearkens back to Future Sound of London’s Dead Cities, while tonally it recalls Murcof’s Rememberanza. Adriano Zanni‘s vision of a future world is the cold reflection of a present reality in which many places are already deserted: peeling houses, dilapidated storefronts, bombed villages. At one time, they teemed with life. Once humans have no more use for a city, they abandon it, leaving only rubble and questionable specters. The reasons may be as far afield as the loss of jobs, the evaporation of resources, or a campaign of bombs. More than anything, Post Dub Cities is an album of mood. Zanni wants his listeners to be uncomfortable, to regard these cities as one does the stone wreckage of Ozymandius. From the opening notes of “Crisopoli” (also the first single), he casts a spell of resignation and despair. The pace is slow, but not sluggish; the beats restrained, but not soft. Someone has to bear witness. In “Pyramiden,” the tone grows harsher, with amplified whispers, clacking pipes and cavernous echoes. Were it not for the dub timbres, one might call this industrial or post-industrial music. Each piece seems to hide another piece behind it: a subdued rhythm, a moving shadow. In “Centralia,” sharp beats stumble like scavengers sifting through wreckage. These visitors may not be human, or even humanoid; in Alan Weisman’s classic The World Without Us, everything from roaches to raccoons reclaims its own. Rust abrades metal; girders bend; branches break through glass. The accompanying pdf is essential to the release. Referencing Calvino and Marcelli, Zanni writes of the empty city as an “echo chamber,” an image reflected in the music. A hundred pages of sublime black and white photographs follow, captured in cities around the world over the past two decades. The unifying feature is the lack of any human presence, as if scrubbed from existence (insert sci-fi theory here). Proof of humanity’s presence remains, but without context. In Zanni’s own words: “memory without recollection, structure without use, body without inhabitants.” In response, the music is architectural: one imagines a grid in which beats and notes are purposely placed. Belgrade, Vienna, Amsterdam, Barcelona, Berlin, Dublin, Sarajevo, Rome, London, Prague, Madrid, Krakow, Istanbul, Lisbon, Palermo and more, all deserted: buildings empty, rollercoasters stilled, markets abandoned, art left to dissolve. Not a single vehicle is visible, even on the highway. One can see what humans have done, but not where they have gone. In what seems to be the final image, a massive wall of chairs is ready for a group of patrons who never arrive. Capturing these images must have required remarkable patience and timing. The last bonus track, “San Zhi Pod City,” offers a surprise: the appearance of a human voice. Even this turns out to be a loop, a remnant, an echo. But Zanni does have a final trick up his sleeve: on page 99, the people reappear, filling the square. The last four images show humanity wall to literal wall: perhaps too much humanity, suggesting a reason for its removal or demise. As much as one pores through “Kadykchan” and “San Zhi Pod City” for a matching restoration, one cannot hear it in the grooves. The listener is left to ponder whether the detritus of humanity might hold any intrinsic value, or if it is only sound and fury, signifying nothing. (Richard Allen)
items._cn_summary: Adriano Zanni的《Post Dub Cities》以未来废弃城市为意象，将dub质感与后工业电子融合，打造出充满冷漠与废墟感的氛围专辑。作品节奏缓慢却非慵懒，节拍克制而具张力，回响、回声与管道敲击声塑造出空洞的回音室效果。专辑配有百页黑白摄影集，呈现欧洲多座废弃城市中无人却留有人造痕迹的场景，音乐与影像互为映照。末曲中唯一出现的人声最终被揭示为循环采样，呼应整张专辑"无人的记忆"的核心命题。整体在概念深度、声音设计与跨媒介结合上均展现出明确的艺术意图。

items.body: In Passage, some of the most elemental transitions are embraced and explored using sound to portray some complex and undefined spiritual concepts. The concept behind Passage is that of passing from one phase of your life to another. This may include new residences, changing relationships, traveling to an entirely different solar system, or passing on from this life to whatever may be next. This strange dark new place possibly extends forever Passage by Chris Meyer's Alias Zone featuring Robert Rich   Alias Zone is the cinematic tribal electronic music project of Chris Meyer of Learning Modular. Chris combines unique sounds crafted on his modular synthesizers with field recordings, hand percussion, and other elements in a unique, melodic fashion. I would tell you that the cavern here has no bottom, instead the earth is hollow, there are the sounds of very few strange forces moving about, these are their stories. In Passage, some of the most elemental transitions are embraced and explored using sound to portray some complex and undefined spiritual concepts. The concept behind Passage is that of passing from one phase of your life to another. This may include new residences, changing relationships, traveling to an entirely different solar system, or passing on from this life to whatever may be next. Each slowly-unfolding piece is its own cinematic journey, inviting you to explore Alias Zone’s dreamscapes and imaginary worlds. This time, for Passage, Alias Zone features ambient music legend Robert Rich, who began building his own analog modular synthesizers in 1976, when he was 13, and later studied computer music at Stanford‘s CCRMA while researching lucid dreaming. Working in a wide array of the arts and with over 40 albums spanning four decades, his all-night Sleep ​Concerts opened up the performance of audio arts into a fundamentally whole new dimension. Robert Rich‘s solos on Passage illustrate a series of slow, meditative journeys featuring lush, organic landscapes and waterways, which weave their way through Alias Zone‘s backdrops of quiet industrial decay. Emerging shadows convey powerful stories from the biggest caverns. For Passage, Chris has chosen his custom modular synthesizer, Korg Wavestation, ASM Hydrasynth, Folktek Nano Garden, gong growls, slow-motion rattles & bells. Robert brings his Haken Continuum with eoWave Metallik Resonator, Vibraslide guitar, PVC flute, Expressive E Osmose. This strange dark new place possibly extends forever. Let us commit to continue into the perfect darkness. We are just entering the cavern, the way is dark and we are the first after all these centuries. The old cave has a huge deep pool, the spirits take the forms of water sprites, naiads and undines. I cannot see anything, but I can hear so much, here we are at peace and in balance. Somehow things move slowly when they are this big. The first ceremony has already begun and it continues. “Elegy” (12:13) sets the opening trajectory, we are in the great hall leading to the abyss. After the ceremony usually the previously hidden inner being affirms the change. What I know for sure is that strange things can happen deep in these caves, we can listen and then let them rest. I hear the calls of eyeless creatures of the darkness, I think that all the water spirits are still here, but with a new message. Things get more complex, we are in a sleepy string forest haunted by a theremin-like night rider, “Realization” (17:31) comes into focus. I am dropping a rock into the dark hole and it never hits bottom. After all, we are getting deeper into the cave, travelling for miles and miles. The flute embraces us, and calms us, now it gets quiet. Beyond this place the territory is infinite, and the circumstances change. In the end, the drones melt back into the void. We continue to slowly drift off into oblivion :: The third track, “Horizonless” (15:45) starts, we are hanging out in the bigger cave, there is a construction site in here, too not very close, I hear bubbles swirl, maybe there is deep water, the flute glows, metal tings and rings and the constant listener just floats there. These must be the ancient bells that were once found on the bottom of the old cave. In the  darkness, on a zephyr, the irregular sounds of banging metal clangs in the distance and get loud sometimes. We are kept afloat upon the water sounds and the flute. Who can imagine what they are building out there? We continue to slowly drift off into oblivion. Next we come to “Afterlife (The Three Gates)” (12:58), it sounds like we are passing further down. There is no hurry, I might hear spooky chanting monks beyond the veil. The cenobites are always heading further down into the caverns below, now they are taking us along. Slowly descending. As bowed strings shimmer and echo, I begin to look for signs of the three gates. This must be where the dead people are. Now I know, here is where they keep the real darkness. Chris Meyers has been making electronic music since he was a teenager in the late 1970s. He has designed electronic music synthesizers and digital recording devices for companies including Sequential Circuits and Roland, such as creating the Vector Synthesis sound generation technique. His first album under the name Alias Zone was chosen by AFIM as the best independent electronic/new age album in 2002. The core tracks for Passage came out of an invitation to play a two-hour ambient concert as part of Currents Gallery 826’s Vibrant Pool exhibit, where five different artists – Chris Meyer’s Alias Zone, Jim Coker of Meridian Alpha, Trovarsi, Jason Fink, and Anthony Ballo – performed simultaneously in different rooms of the gallery. Chris recorded his many hours of exploratory improvisations as well as his performance the night of the exhibit, and edited them down to four extended soundscapes. He then passed these pieces on to long-time friend Robert Rich, who notes: “When Chris sent me the raw tracks for his next album, he gave me open permission to try anything. I told him he could delete or modify anything I sent. I responded intuitively, after listening closely to the modes inherent in the pieces, and then charting out harmonic ideas within those pitch spaces. Each piece seemed to ask for a different approach, yet I also wanted to stay somewhat experimental to respond appropriately to the music. I intended my resulting improvised performances to thread between simple and slightly chaotic, to respond to the abstraction in the original tracks.” Robert ended up choosing a Haken Continuum, Vibraslide guitar, PVC flute, and Expressive E Osmose to play over the four tracks. Chris then recorded additional percussion instruments – growl gongs and “slow motion” rattles and bells – on three of the tracks in response to Robert’s solos. The result is a unique collection of sonic worlds which works as an ambient aural environment for meditation or contemplation, as well as for attentive listening and mental exploration. Passage is available on Bandcamp. Passage by Chris Meyer's Alias Zone featuring Robert RichThe post Chris Meyer’s Alias Zone featuring Robert Rich :: Passage (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以"过渡"为核心概念，通过模块化合成器与田野录音、手工打击乐等元素，探索从生命一个阶段过渡到另一阶段的复杂精神主题。Alias Zone 是 Chris Meyer 的电影感部落电子项目，他使用定制模块化合成器、Korg Wavestation、ASM Hydrasynth 等设备创造出独特的旋律质感。专辑特邀氛围音乐传奇人物 Robert Rich 合作，他带来 Haken Continuum、eWave 金属谐振器、Vibraslide 吉他等非常规乐器。Rich 的独奏段落呈现出缓慢冥想般的旅程，织体丰富的有机景观与水道穿行于 Alias Zone 所营造的寂静工业衰败背景之中。每一首曲目都是一场缓慢展开的电影之旅，邀请听众进入想象中的梦境世界。乐器配置与声音设计极具实验性，将部落节奏、氛围音景与现代合成器技术融为一体，形成跨越类型边界的独特听觉体验。

items.body: In a house in Lomé, a woman kept a set of ceremonial pots she used for preparing potions for the older women of the Vodun temples. Vodun is the West African religion the Ewe and Fon have practised across Togo and Benin for centuries, the one that crossed the Atlantic on slave ships and became Haitian Vodou and Louisiana Voodoo. Its spirits are bound up with natural forces and they are reached through drumming and singing, so those women sang constantly. Her grandson grew up believing all that singing had gone into the clay and stayed there. Years later he took the pots and built a drum kit out of them. His name is Toto Tchilatchi, and half of what Nana Benz du Togo carry onto a stage is those pots. The other half is a bass David Kasanku built out of PVC drainpipe. He used to play bass, then spent four years assembling the gazé tuyau. Once it went underneath Toto’s kit, the pots and drums came to life, and together they made a groove full of sub-bass and complex polyrhythms. That groove became the bedrock for three singers, Lady Apoc, Parus Kekeli and Izealedu, with a small vintage Korg keyboard alongside their voices. The band’s word for what all of it adds up to is trance. They describe Vodun itself as being about rhythm, trance, nature and connection, and Lady Apoc says theirs comes from “repetitive energy.“ None of the five knew each other until 2019, when Peter Solo, the leader of Vaudou Game, came to Lomé to run a workshop and brought local musicians and artists together for it. Out of that workshop came the band, and Solo has produced them ever since. They took their name from the Nana Benz, the wax-print traders of Lomé’s central market who drove Mercedes-Benz cars and were confided in by the powerful. The band say they admire the courage and force those women showed in patriarchal societies. They sing in English, French and Mina, over the Vodun scales of the snake, Dan, and of Mami Wata, about women and the earth, and they say protecting one is inseparable from protecting the other. Their feminism, the band say, comes from the strength and resilience of African women, and their ecology from Vodun itself, and they say protecting women and protecting the earth cannot be pulled apart. Like many people of their generation, they grew up with mixed feelings about Vodun and were taught to be ashamed of parts of it, and at some point they moved away from it. Going back gave them their voice back. They stopped trying to fit into a musical category and started creating from who they are. Even so, they never set out to put Vodun in the spotlight, and years of work in the shadows came before they dared to get on a stage. Their first concert in Europe was Transmusicales de Rennes in 2022, and AGO followed the year after, recorded at the OTODI studio in Lomé with Solo producing. They went back to OTODI in December 2024 to record SÉ NAM, again with Solo, and it came out in June 2025. Its eleven tracks have a more contemporary production and more room for groove and rhythm. The title means “understand me” in Mina, one of the three languages they sing in. In October they bring it to WOMEX in Las Palmas… For this episode of Musical Road to WOMEX they answered our questions about how Vodun meets the dancefloor, what their handmade instruments do and what they hope to find on the island: they want to hear the timple, meet local musicians and find out what traces of African and Atlantic exchange can still be heard in Canarian music, and they arrive, as they put it, with their ears open. The playlist at the end lets you hear what they are bringing. You’ve been described as pioneers of “digital voodoo”. For someone hearing you for the first time, how would you introduce the meeting of Vodun tradition and the dancefloor? For us, Digital Vodou is not about taking something old and trying to make it modern. It is about showing that Vodun is already alive and has always had the power to evolve. Vodun is about rhythm, trance, nature and connection. And the dancefloor can be a place for that too. People come together, move together, let go. We bring traditional rhythms, songs, percussion and the handmade instruments we create into electronic music, bass and contemporary sounds. For us, it is a meeting between something very old and something that is still being born. That is what makes it feel both ancestral and futuristic. The band takes its name from the Nana Benz, the market women who turned the wax-print trade into power and independence. What did diving back into your Vodun heritage, after leaving it behind, open up for you musically? It gave us our voice back. Like many people from our generation, we grew up with mixed feelings about Vodun. There were things we were taught to be ashamed of, so at some point we moved away from it. Coming back to it changed the way we saw ourselves. We realised that Vodun is not only a spiritual tradition. It is also a way of understanding our relationship with the earth, with women, with our ancestors and with each other. And musically, it opened a whole world for us: rhythms, melodies, stories, symbols. Things that were already inside us. We stopped trying to fit into a musical category. We started creating from who we really are. WOMEX lands this year in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, an Atlantic island whose own traditions ride on the timple, a five-string guitar that carries both African and Latin American trade routes. What are you most curious to discover there? We are curious about the connections between the different traditions. Islands are special places. Cultures arrive there, meet, change and survive. We want to hear the timple, meet local musicians and discover what traces of African and Atlantic exchanges can still be heard in Canarian music. And honestly, we are excited about the unexpected. Maybe one of our handmade instruments will meet a sound from the island in a way we never imagined. That is what we love about music. Your instruments are handmade and upcycled, the gazé tuyaux among them, and your themes are feminist and ecological. In a WOMEX programme full of traditions, what makes your sound and your message unmistakably yours? For us, everything is connected. The recycled instruments are not just something you see on stage. They are part of our sound and part of the way we think. We take things that people throw away and give them another life. In a way, we do the same with our stories and traditions. We take things that have been misunderstood or pushed aside and bring them back into the present. Our feminism comes from the strength and resilience of African women. And our connection to ecology comes from Vodun itself. We often say, “Whoever does not respect women does not respect nature.” For us, that says a lot about who Nana Benz Du Togo is. WOMEX is built on unexpected meetings. Which artists, labels or collaborators are you hoping to cross paths with in Las Palmas? We don’t really have a list of names. We want to meet people who are deeply connected to where they come from but are not afraid to experiment. Artists who can move between tradition, ritual, electronic music, performance and new ideas. And that is one of the things we love about WOMEX. You can have a conversation with someone backstage and suddenly discover that there is something you can create together. We are coming with our ears open. You’ve toured Europe and built a reputation as a live force. Does a room of delegates and music professionals change how you bring the trance and the groove of your set? Not really. Of course, we know that WOMEX is important and that there will be a lot of professionals in the room. But once we are on stage, we have to be ourselves. Whether there are one hundred people, a thousand people or music professionals watching us, we want the same thing: for people to feel the music in their bodies. We want them to forget for a moment who they are supposed to be and simply become part of the rhythm. That is when the magic happens. “Voodoo is Nature,” you’ve said. Gran Canaria is a volcanic island shaped by the ocean around it. Does a landscape like that speak to the ecology at the heart of your songs? Absolutely. When you see a volcanic landscape, you are reminded that the earth is alive. It is powerful, it changes, it moves. For us, nature is not something outside of us. In Vodun, it is a living presence. The ocean, the wind, the stone, the fire inside the earth, these are not just things around us. They are forces. So being on an island shaped by the ocean and volcanoes feels very familiar to our way of thinking. It reminds us that we are part of something much bigger than ourselves. Your work carries a clear message about women’s strength and respect for the planet. Is there something you feel especially compelled to say through this showcase? Yes. We want to remind people that protecting women and protecting the earth are not separate things. We believe our traditions can still teach us something about that balance. We are not trying to go back to the past. We are trying to understand what we can take from it to imagine a different future. For us, women are creators, transmitters, protectors and forces of transformation. That is something we want to celebrate through our music. After SÉ NAM, what’s next? New recordings, new collaborations, directions you’re keen to push the project toward? SÉ NAM was an important chapter for us, but we already feel the next one coming. We are working on new music and pushing the dialogue between ritual percussion, the instruments we make ourselves and electronic production even further. We also want to work with artists from other parts of Africa, the Caribbean and Latin America. There are so many shared histories, rhythms and spiritual connections across the Atlantic that we would love to explore. We want to keep moving forward without losing our roots. If you could write a personal invitation to the people of Las Palmas to come and discover your showcase, what would it say? Come with your body before your expectations. Come to dance, listen, feel and maybe remember something older than all of us. We are bringing rhythms from Togo, women’s voices, handmade instruments and the energy of Digital Vodou. Don’t just come and watch us. Come and experience it with us. If you join us, we will create the ceremony together.   On 23 October at the Plaza Stage in Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Nana Benz du Togo will ask the WOMEX crowd to forget for a moment who they are supposed to be and become part of the rhythm   PLAYLIST: NANA BENZ DU TOGO X RHYTHM PASSPORT   You can find all the previous episodes of Musical Road to Womex HERE   The post Musical Road to WOMEX 2026 – Nana Benz du Togo appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑围绕多哥洛美Vodun宗教仪式音乐展开，核心乐器极具独创性：鼓手将祖母用于调配祭祀药水的陶罐改造成鼓组，贝斯手则用PVC排水管自制低音提琴。陶罐的泥土共鸣与管材次低音相结合，形成复杂的复合节奏律动，构成三位人声与一台复古Korg键盘的底座。乐队从Vodun传统中汲取蛇、Dan、Mami Wata等音阶，用英语、法语和米纳语演唱，主题聚焦女性力量与生态保护的不可分割性。制作人Peter Solo来自Vaudou Game，在洛美OTODI录音棚完成录制。作品将西非仪式音乐传统与当代世界音乐制作理念融合，节奏设计层次丰富，人声编排充满恍惚感，既保留了宗教音乐的灵性内核，又通过自造乐器和现代录音手段开辟出独特的听觉空间。

items.body: Band: Sigh | Album: Goh-Ka | Genre: Progressive metal | Year: 2026 From: Tokyo, Japan | Label: Peaceville For fans of: Enslaved, Between the Buried and Me, Opeth Bandcamp Sigh is one of the longest-running and most influential progressive metal bands out there. Starting off as a symphonic black metal band in the early 1990s, they quickly took a more experimental turn and never looked back. Goh-Ka is the band’s 14th full-length release (or 13th, if you want to categorize last year’s re-recording of their 2007 album, Hangman’s Hymn, a little differently). This album is based on kusōzu, a Japanese artform depicting the nine stages of decay described in Buddhism. These are used as a means of meditation on impermanence. The music here sticks to Sigh’s usual style. But where the last album of theirs I listened to–Shiki–left me unimpressed, this is one of their strongest outings. Avant-garde, progressive, and Japanese folk elements play large parts on this album, and the use of recurring musical themes ties everything together. Japanese folk was more prominent than usual on Shiki, and that trend continues here. Goh-Ka opens with the nine-minute “Kuso-shi 1, 2, and 3”. Sigh’s signature synth tones weave and burble amid heavy guitar lines, accented with traditional Japanese instrumentation. This cut is relatively restrained by Sigh’s standards, but that degree of focus pays off here. The power of the music is apparent, and the band’s decision to up the Japonic elements helps this to stand out. The shifts between avant-garde metal, organ-fueled prog, and Japanese folk are fluid and organic. “Jigoku-Zoshi 1: Unkamusho” has an anxious opening with some nearly-Latin-sounding percussion. But soon enough it plunges into melodic black metal with speedy synth flourishes and classical-influenced guitar lines. This is classic Sigh, and it’s a lot of fun. Things slow down on “Anzenshokon”. Acoustic guitar, flute, and clean vocals lend this a mournful feel in its opening. Crushing, doomy guitars burst in on occasion to punctuate the verses, and psychedelic production adds a dreamlike quality, all of which do an incredible job at evoking a corpse rotting in a field, but in a reflective way. In the last couple minutes, the band incorporates obvious early King Crimson influences for a dramatic conclusion. “Kuso-shi 4, 5, and 6” comes next, opening with lush, symphonic doom metal tones. The drumming here (and elsewhere on the album) is stellar, with lots of fancy fills and flourishes. A sinister acoustic passage follows this, evoking some of Opeth’s better quiet moments. Themes from parts 1-3 are revisited here, as are the psychedelic acoustic tones of the preceding song, adding a sense of cohesion. I really like the intermingling of electric and acoustic elements. Not only are Japanese instruments used (maybe it’s a shamisen? Or a koto? I’m not sure.), but some Western-style classical guitar shows up, as well. This is a lurching, foreboding composition that highlights all this band’s best tendencies. “Shoso” is an eerie, one-minute electronic instrumental interlude that leads right into “Unputenpu”. This is a savage, biting composition that sees guitar and shamisen harmonizing beneath raving vocals. Melodic moments contrast against this, and Mikael Åkerfeldt of Opeth shows up to provide a solo. I really love the unorthodox percussion choices deployed during the chorus. Some sinister synth and shamisen open up “Jinmenjushen” as the band dips back into some slower riffage. The verses are much more energetic, though, focusing on melodic black metal, sometimes bordering on black ‘n’ roll. There’s a clear sense of drama here with the group vocals during the chorus, and some unexpected saxophone harmonizes with synthesizer during a particularly exciting instrumental break. This is a breakneck composition that hardly takes its foot off the accelerator once things get going. The final minute does slow down a bit, but there’s no lack of intensity. “Jigoku-Zoshi 2: Tokatsujigoku” immediately bursts forth with powerful black metal. The drumming is again a highlight here. The chorus of this song dips into avant-garde orchestral elements. I’d compare this to some of BTBAM’s odder songs, but Sigh’s been doing weird metal for much longer than those guys. A pair of sub-two-minute songs follow. “Kushukankyo” feels Andean, with breathy flute, gently strummed guitar, and understated hand percussion. It’s a wonderful little breather. “Kuso-shi 7”, on the other hand, consists mostly of sound effects and weird synthesizer bloops.  The album closes on its longest song, the 11-minute “Kuso-shi 8 and 9 / Mettaijakujo”. After a dramatic, theatrical opening, the first verse is relatively grounded. Acoustic and electric passages contrast wonderfully. Dashes of electronic and psychedelic music crop up amid the crushing riffs. Plenty of bands throw things together and hope they work; Sigh is one of the bands that best integrates strange inclusions in a way that makes sense. Folk elements, topped with big, melodic guitar lines lead off the second half of this song. More musical themes from earlier in the record are revisited in a satisfying way. Rock elements eventually melt away altogether as this piece enters its final movement. Orchestral music takes over in a macabre march, eventually dissolving into a synthesizer drone. After some warbling static, the album ends on a warm and peaceful electric piano passage, underscoring the overall concept of this album: accepting the impermanence of life. Goh-Ka is another excellent work from Sigh. Everything here is lively and played with so much passion. The band does an amazing job at varying tempo and texture, and their ability to change direction so suddenly and skillfully is always impressive. Score: 96/100
items._genre: progressive metal / avant-garde / Japanese folk / symphonic black metal
items._cn_summary: Sigh 第十四张全长专辑以佛教九尸图为概念，将日本传统器乐与前卫金属融合。九分钟开场曲在合成器音织与重型吉他之间编织东方民谣元素，后半段多首作品以悲怆原声吉他与毒舌般的死亡金属音色交替推进。评论特别指出日式民谣比重较以往明显提升，传统器乐与管风琴式前卫段落、迷幻声效之间的转换流畅自然。器乐编排以多组器乐主题的反复变奏贯穿全作，形成统一结构。多首作品的曲名与佛学九阶段腐败相对应，歌词与器乐共同营造出一种沉思式的腐败美学。评论认为这是乐队近年来最强作品之一，前作未能留下深刻印象，而这作在聚焦与日式元素的强化上取得显著成功。

items.album: John Coltrane 100: Live at the Village Vanguard
items.excerpt: John Coltrane – Live at the Village Vanguard (Impulse, 1997) By Kenneth Blanchard There are certain recordings that stretched my grasp of jazz (and indeed music). Andrew Hill’s Point of Departure comes to mind. Coltrane’s LVV collection is another. Recorded over four nights in 1961 at the Jerusalem of Jazz, only five of the originally recorded numbers were released in the following two years. The 1997 box set is a genuine treasure. The structure of the music remains within standard hop bop space
items.body: John Coltrane – Live at the Village Vanguard (Impulse, 1997) By Kenneth Blanchard There are certain recordings that stretched my grasp of jazz (and indeed music). Andrew Hill’s Point of Departure comes to mind. Coltrane’s LVV collection is another. Recorded over four nights in 1961 at the Jerusalem of Jazz, only five of the originally recorded numbers were released in the following two years. The 1997 box set is a genuine treasure. The structure of the music remains within standard hop bop spaces, but the moods blossom into an entirely new ecosystem. The inclusion of Eric Dolphy was one of Trane’s most brilliant moves. On Naima, Spiritual, India , his low horns (also sax and bass clarinet) perfectly match Trane’s tenor and soprano sax. Trane’s interest in alternative spiritual and musical traditions is obvious enough. His famous “sheets of sound” slide in and out of every line. I find the articulation of Coltrane’s own personality to be as vivid here as on any of his recordings. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑收录了约翰·科尔特兰1961年在Village Vanguard俱乐部连续四个晚上的现场录音，原版仅发行了五首曲目，而1997年的盒装套装将更多内容完整呈现。乐评指出，这些录音极大地拓展了作者对爵士乃至音乐的认知边界。音乐结构仍保持在bop的框架内，但情绪和氛围延展至一个全新的生态系统。埃里克·多尔菲的加入是科尔特兰最具慧眼的决定之一，他在多首曲目中的低音域演奏（包括低音单簧管和低音 saxophone）与科尔特兰的次中音和高音 sax 形成精妙呼应。科尔特兰对替代性精神传统和音乐传统的兴趣在此清晰可辨，标志性的"声幕"技法贯穿每一条乐句的进出。这是展现科尔特兰个人性格最为鲜明的录音之一。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._genre: avant-garde / ambient / experimental / contemporary classical / protest song
items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz 与作曲家 Francesco Paolo Paladino 及诗人 Luca Chino Ferrari 合作的专辑《Songs of Compassion》，收录十一首作品。音乐以钢琴为核心，叠加弦乐、木管与合成器音色，形成非线性、模态化的音响结构，既非传统和声进行也非流行旋律模式，被比作 Steve Reich 而非 Steve Stills 的创作路径。Moskowitz 的演唱不拘于对角线和声，而是让旋律服从每个词的意义，钢琴本身充当第二个声部甚至评论者角色。歌词延续六十年代抗议歌曲传统，《Pale Wanderer》剖析威权主义的共谋机制，《Charlottesville》以共词方式直面新纳粹集会场景，同时也有对死亡与宇宙位置的冥想。整张专辑是1960年代实验乐队 The United States of America 精神在当下政治分裂语境中的延续，形式与内容相互支撑。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: Tako Toki 这张专辑的核心在于他们亲手用废旧物品制作乐器——包括被称作 tassofons、clarinuts、kitchenofon 等自创乐器。乐评指出，这些 DIY 乐器在录音中表现出惊人的音准与音质，甚至能精准模仿传统管乐与打击乐的音色。在音乐风格上，专辑融合了克莱兹默、昆比亚、非洲节拍、桑巴、中东旋律等多种世界音乐元素，每首曲目对应一种文化灵感来源，乐器配置也与之匹配。乐曲包含大量即兴段落，展现出演奏者扎实的技术功底。整张专辑传递出一个核心理念：音乐的本质在于创造声音的欲望，而非依赖精良的乐器。乐评将该专辑视为对音乐本质的庆祝，同时也反思了当代乐器过剩与音乐创造力之间的关系。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是挪威Camilla Hole Trio在融合探索上的最新尝试，将传统挪威民间舞曲素材置于爵士即兴的框架中重新审视。主创Camilla Hole以高音萨克斯为核心乐器，与贝斯手Egil Kalman和鼓手/颤音琴演奏者Knut Kvifte Nesheim组成的三人组合打破了传统乐队角色分配——器乐声部在即兴中不断轮换、交织与解构。Kalman的模块化合成器与Nesheim的颤音琴以叠录方式为原声基底增添色彩层次，使作品在保留了民间旋律骨架的同时，呈现出开放而流动的即兴质感。整体手法延续了乐队上一张专辑中科幻合成器与民俗素材结合的实验方向，但更趋沉稳、内省，聚焦于本土民间音乐与当代爵士语汇之间的对话。

items.body: Achachay is what highland Ecuadorians say when the cold catches them, arraray when the heat does. Both words came into Andean Spanish from Quichua, and BRITTA builds “Achachay” on the pair: a love song about wanting someone enough to feel both. A requinto line, the small high-tuned guitar of Ecuadorian string music, runs over percussion drawn from the country’s Pacific coast and a trap low end. The alt-pop production leaves the guitar exposed and the beat holds a steady pressure under a vocal that stays at the point of anticipation. Born in Ambato in the central Ecuadorian Andes and based in Los Angeles in the US, Britta has been feeding Ecuadorian traditional forms into dance production for a while: on her single “NON3 (no te dejes avecilla)” she sampled her own voice singing an albazo, the fast triple-time song form of the Ecuadorian highlands, and built a house track around it. “Achachay” points that same working method at Latin alternative, with the Andean Spanish idioms running through the lyric carrying as much of the song’s identity as the requinto and the percussion do. Listen to “Achachay” HERE The post Daily Discovery: BRITTA – Achachay appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._genre: latin alternative / andean folk fusion / electronic
items._cn_summary: 厄瓜多尔裔洛杉矶制作人BRITTA将安第斯山区传统弦乐（requinto吉他）与太平洋海岸打击乐节奏相融合，并叠加trap低频节拍，构建出一首跨越地域的另类流行作品。歌曲标题源自克丘亚语词汇，歌词中安第斯西班牙语习语与requinto旋律、打击乐层次共同构成其文化身份的核心。制作上保留了吉他裸露的质感，人声保持在期待感的临界点，贝斯线维持稳定的压力感。此前她曾将albazo民歌形式采样后融入house制作，此作则将同样的方法论指向拉丁另类领域，展示其将传统形式持续注入电子舞曲生产的一贯路线。

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — A south Korean group that took 18 years to release their first album and the least one can say isthat Superstring didn't take the easy road. Yes their main influence is classical music, but theywouldn't name have named their kids Ludwig, Johan Sebastian or Wolfgang Amadeus. They might havethought of Edgar, Karlheinz or Gabriel, though. BTW, it's not just about modern classical , as thereare hints of jazz dispersed throughout the duration of their first works. Noteworthy, TGD was firstreleased as vinyl-only, waiting some three years to finally release it in the user-friendly formatcalled CD.Indeed, while relatively dissonant, SS is not extreme Avant Prog like Guapo would be, but they'renot very careful about your sanity beyond your eardrums. Their Grand Design is still relativelyaccessible, if you like atmospheric improvisation, almost cinematic, gloomy ambiances with also PostRock moments. This instrumental quintet will be remarkably stable throughout their career, focusingon the violin and piano as lead instruments, but backed up by a guitar. There are some lovelymoments, but also plenty of tense passages, not necessarily providing a release outlet for thenervous accumulation.TBH, not my cup or tea, but it's definitely worth their Bandcamp detour at least once, even if itwill never be an essential piece of work. Add another half-star, though !!!
items._genre: RIO / avant-prog / contemporary classical / chamber jazz
items._cn_summary: 韩国五人乐团Superstring耗时十八年才推出首张专辑，以小提琴与钢琴为主导乐器，辅以吉他，构建出介于现代古典、即兴爵士与后摇之间的器乐声响。乐评指出专辑受Edgar Varèse、Karlheinz Stockhausen等二十世纪作曲家影响，融合了大气化的即兴段落与近乎电影配乐般的阴郁氛围，偶有后摇滚的爆发时刻。尽管整体偏向不协和，但相对Guapo等极端前卫乐团更易接近。评论者承认该作并非个人偏好，但认为值得在Bandcamp上至少试听一次，并补加半星认可。专辑最初仅以黑胶发行，三年后才推出CD版本，这种发行方式本身也体现了乐团的独立姿态。

items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — There is so much talent involved in making this record that though it escapes the normal blues/psychedelia forms of that era and becomes proggy and avant, it is so easy and fun to listen too. It takes you through so many emotions, it can make you angry, it's bluesy, it's funny at parts (has a track on dedicated to a candy bar).But man, although the musicianship is of course fantastic, Captain's vocal performance makes the real difference here. Just listen to songs like "Where there's woman" , "Grown so ugly", "Autumn's child", or "Electricity" (where he literally broke a microphone while recording it.)Although Zappa was a good friend and inspiration to Captain Beefheart, Captain's music is far more accessible and this album is a good starting point for a listener who wants to discover their music.
items._cn_summary: 这张1967年的专辑打破了当时蓝调与迷幻的常规形态，向前卫与先锋方向延伸。乐队阵容技术精湛，但真正让作品脱颖而出的是主唱极具辨识度的人声演绎——从愤怒到幽默，情绪跨度宽广，据称在录制《Electricity》时甚至当场弄坏了麦克风。整张专辑既保持了可听性与趣味性，又突破了类型边界。相比同期好友Frank Zappa的作品，Captain Beefheart的音乐更容易被普通听众接受，对于想要接触其后续更激进创作的人来说，本作是一个理想的入门切口。

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — SS's second album certainly starts in a WTF, but if Elements of Architecture stretches their TGD debut by a mile, and go the extra-distance to play on the dissonance frontier, but never crossing it. BTW, they must have a fascination about construction design, since their next three releases will mention it on the record sleeves. On the sonic front, it seems that Kim's bass guitar is playing a more prominent role than previously - especially on the title track. In a general way, Kim seems to be the head honcho, handling design & mixing/production, even, if the album is released again on the violinist Dancing Butterfly label. In some moments, via the guitarist, King Crimson is not far away.Definitely a harder grasp on what SS tried to do in this Avant-Post-Prog creation, but if all tracks were more in the mould of Floating Debris, then then they might've gotten that fourth star. .
items._cn_summary: SUPERSTRING的第二张专辑延续了前作的前卫方向，在不协和音的边界上大胆探索但未逾矩，呈现出先锋色彩浓厚的创作路线。贝斯手Kim在制作与混音中占据主导地位，低音线条在同名曲中尤为突出，整体音响设计偏冷峻、结构化，吉他段落隐约呼应King Crimson的质感。专辑以建筑学意象贯穿，呼应了乐队此后多张封套延续的视觉主题。评论者认为作品较前作更难消化，仅有部分曲目如Floating Debris真正触及到了Avant-Post-Prog的佳作水准，未能获得满分评价。作为小厂牌发行的前卫摇滚作品，在融合与实验层面展现出一定野心，但整体可听性仍是限制其评分的关键因素。

items._cn_summary: LAUSBUB以二人编制呈现两张专辑概念迥异的作品：Disc-1收录四首商业语境下的CM曲与电视剧主题曲，呈现大众流行层面；Disc-2则跨越音乐具体派、工业声响、硬核极简、达布至环境音乐的边界，以碎片化的声音素材构建冷冽而俏皮的编辑性听觉拼贴。整体制作由網守将平担任共同制作人、葛西敏彦负责录音工程，延续了自"golden lighter"以来鲜明的模式切换策略——商业面与实验面并行不悖。这种双轨结构既保留了面向主流听众的入口，又在第二碟中释放出对先锋声响美学的探索，将年轻女性视角下的新浪潮节拍与冷酷工业质感相融合，形成属于两人特有的实验性与亲和力并存的声音图景。

items.body: Los Angeles-based ambient explorer stanleycypress finds comfort in smaller spaces with Ephemeral, a two-track slice of life where atmospheric modulations weave through melodic drone tones and cascading Detroit-inflected textures. A melancholic intersection of sound and space Los Angeles-based ambient explorer stanleycypress finds comfort in smaller spaces with Ephemeral, a two-track slice of life where atmospheric modulations weave through melodic drone tones and cascading Detroit-inflected textures—think Rod Modell—across opener “Momentary Drift.” “Trillium,” meanwhile, doubles down on duration and amplitude, its minimal techno and Plastikman-like tentacles revealing a 3 a.m. 313 soundtrack for wandering souls. Isolated highs hover above drowning low-end, before an eventual breakdown gathers every microscopic element and gradually energizes it through its closing minutes, pulling the listener deeper into its hypnotic current. Two tracks steeped in ambient techno propulsion, calm, and control; one piece reflecting another. Together, they form a melancholic intersection of sound and space, a flow that feels just right at just over ten minutes, yet could easily drift infinitely. Ephemeral is available on Bandcamp. Ephemeral by stanleycypressThe post stanleycypress :: Ephemeral EP (Self Released) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._genre: ambient / ambient techno / drone / minimal techno
items._cn_summary: 洛杉矶环境音乐制作人stanleycypress在两张短曲中呈现了克制而精密的氛围声响。第一曲以大气调制与旋律性嗡鸣交织，融入底特律系质感，音墙低缓铺展，孤立的高频浮于低频之上。第二曲延伸了时长与振幅，呈现极简techno节奏脉络，末段将所有微观元素汇聚并逐步推升能量，构筑催眠般的下沉感。整张EP以简短篇幅（十余分钟）勾勒出忧郁的声场交汇点，气氛沉静却暗藏流动的张力，体现出对环境techno节奏推进与音色控制的扎实把握。
