items.body: There was a useful logic to the running order of Friday night’s show at Klub Łącznik. Antibody, Agonoize and System Noire all make music designed to work physically, but they approach that physicality from quite different directions. Antibody built movement through rhythm and the almost compulsive momentum of hard electronic dance music. Agonoize converted it into confrontation, theatrical violence and direct exchange between performer and crowd. System Noire then expanded the same basic principle into something broader and increasingly combustible, combining electronic force with the dynamics of a full band. The evening became an accumulation of different ways of controlling a room. The concert was part of the 2026 run pairing Agonoize with System Noire, with Antibody as special guest; for System Noire, the tour also marks the Hanover band’s 10th anniversary. The Wrocław date was officially scheduled at Klub Łącznik, the concert space within Czasoprzestrzeń at the former Dąbie tram depot. Antibody Photos: Karo Kratochwil Antibody opened the evening, and first a small correction worth making because the name is easily mangled: the project is the work of Jan Laustroer. Laustroer began Antibody in 2013, when he was only twelve, and over the following years developed a sound drawing on industrial, power noise, dark electro and the harder end of rave and hardcore. The debut album Opera of Death appeared in 2017, while the more recent Never Quite Right was released in 2024. In January this year Antibody also collaborated with Grendel on “The Ranidae.” What worked especially well in Wrocław was that none of this required the opening slot to pretend it was already the climax of the night. Antibody’s set was extremely danceable, rhythmically insistent and immediately mobile. The tracks worked through repetition, sharp changes of pressure and bass strong enough to make the body respond before there was much reason to analyse what was happening. It was energetic without becoming shapeless; Jan understands that hard electronic music needs more than volume and speed if it is supposed to sustain movement. The visual presentation supported that. Against a star-filled background, the recurring frogs added a deliberately absurd signature to a set otherwise built around hard, mechanical momentum. They have become an immediately recognisable part of Antibody’s visual vocabulary, and after this year’s Grendel collaboration The Ranidae, their presence felt even more appropriate. There was something rather charming about the collision: pounding industrial rhythm underneath, a small amphibian mythology unfolding behind it. As an opener, Antibody did exactly what was needed. The set did not simply “warm up” the audience in the conventional sense; it established movement as the evening’s basic mode of communication. By the time it ended, the room was no longer waiting for the main acts. Agonoize Photos: Karo Kratochwil The change was immediately visible when Agonoize came on. The space in front of the stage became noticeably denser, bodies moved closer together, and the kind of dancing established during Antibody’s set turned into something more collective and more aggressive. Agonoize were formed in Berlin in 2002 and have spent more than two decades making the relationship between harsh electronic music and extreme stage performance central to their identity. Their current touring page explicitly designated the Wrocław concert as a “Blutshow”, continuing the use of theatrical blood that has long been part of the band’s live language. Their most recent full studio album remains Revelation Six Six Sick, released through RepoRecords in April 2021. Calling what happened at Łącznik simply “brutal” would miss why the set worked. The force was carefully organised. The electronics were dense, abrasive and extremely physical, but they also retained enough rhythmic definition for the material to still work as dance music. Chris L.’s performance depends heavily on this ambiguity: he confronts the audience while simultaneously demanding its participation. And participate they did. The stage blood is obviously theatrical, but the reaction it produces is real. Chris repeatedly showered the front of the audience with it, leaving faces and clothes streaked red, and the people closest to the stage seemed delighted to become part of the spectacle. The distinction is important. Agonoize’s blood show does not function particularly well when treated as something happening to a passive crowd. In Wrocław it became reciprocal. People moved forward knowing very well what was coming. They danced harder, reached towards the stage and quite visibly enjoyed being pulled inside the performance. That made the visual violence feel less like decoration attached to the songs and more like an extension of their physical logic. Chris’s gestures were large and confrontational because the music required a body capable of matching its exaggeration. The show continually crossed the line between concert and grotesque theatre without allowing the theatrical element to weaken the musical one. The encore shifted the visual vocabulary again. Chris returned wearing wings, and after so much aggression, blood and pressure, the image had a surprisingly different weight. It was beautiful precisely because the evening had not prepared us for beauty in any conventional form. The wings did not suddenly turn the performance sentimental; they introduced another register into a stage language that had spent most of the set emphasising impact and provocation. My conversation with Chris afterwards changed how I thought about the performance even further. We had previously discussed his long absence following a very serious illness, but hearing him describe the extent of the recovery in person gave that history a different scale. He spoke about having to rebuild abilities that most people never consciously think about, including basic everyday tasks and forms of recognition, through an exhausting rehabilitation process. I would not want to turn illness into an inspirational narrative imposed on the concert, because that would reduce both the person and the performance. But it does change the meaning of what one has just witnessed. Returning to a stage is one thing. Returning to this kind of stage presence, where the performance demands constant physical engagement, vocal force, timing, theatrical control and the ability to command a densely packed room, is something else. The striking thing was not simply that Chris was back. It was the absence of caution in the performance. In our recent interview, he told me that he has nothing to prove to anyone except himself and that what he wants, fundamentally, is simply to continue making music. Watching this set, that statement became much less abstract. The stamina was visible, certainly, but more important was the appetite behind it. This did not look like someone tentatively reclaiming an old position. It looked like someone fully inhabiting it again. System Noire Photos: Karo Kratochwil If Agonoize generated the evening’s most theatrical violence, System Noire converted the accumulated energy into something broader and, by the end, almost unruly. The Hanover project was founded in 2016 and is celebrating its tenth anniversary this year. Its current formation has grown beyond the original electronic core, and the band’s recent material increasingly allows guitars and a harder industrial-metal edge to interfere with its dark-electro and EBM foundations. Their 2024 album Aftermath includes ten tracks and was followed in February 2025 by Lost Control, whose single version the band themselves describe as harder and more guitar-driven, while a separate club edit strips it back towards electronics. That tension between programmed precision and a more volatile live-band attack was exactly what made the final set work. By this stage the audience no longer needed persuading. Smoke filled the stage, the lighting became much more aggressive, and the room that Antibody had initially taught to move and Agonoize had pushed into increasingly physical participation now had very little reserve left. System Noire used that. Their music has enough melodic architecture to keep the songs readable even when the performance becomes extremely dense. That mattered here. The combination of electronics, forceful vocals, percussion and the heavier edges of the current sound could easily have collapsed into undifferentiated volume; instead, the rhythmic centre remained very clear. People could dance to it. The lighting and smoke also worked unusually well with that construction. They were not merely there to make the stage appear “dark”. Smoke repeatedly altered what could actually be seen: musicians emerged, disappeared and reappeared as the lights cut through it, creating a visual equivalent of the music’s own alternation between defined melodic lines and heavier blocks of sound. And gradually the whole thing became wonderfully disorderly. By the final part of the set, the dancefloor was no longer behaving like a room of individuals politely occupying their allotted space. Movement propagated through it. People were dancing hard, responding to the band and to one another, and the distinction between observing the show and physically participating in it had largely disappeared. Calling it carnage is not much of an exaggeration, although it was an exceptionally friendly form of carnage. System Noire therefore made sense as the final band, even though Agonoize might initially appear the more obvious dramatic climax. Their set did not need to out-provoke what had come before it. Instead, it took the accumulated kinetic energy of the entire evening and gave it somewhere to go. Klub Łącznik Photos: Karo Kratochwil Klub Łącznik itself deserves some credit for why the evening felt so comfortable despite the intensity inside. The venue sits within Czasoprzestrzeń at the former Dąbie tram depot, and its layout provides something particularly useful for this kind of scene event: a clear separation between the physical density of the concert hall and the open area outside. Inside, there is a proper concrete-floored club space where a hard-electronic show can become as loud, smoky and physically crowded as it needs to be. Outside, the yard changes the social rhythm completely. Between sets people could step out, cool down, talk, meet friends and, importantly, encounter the musicians without the strange separation that larger venues often create between audience and performers. That mattered more than it might sound. A night involving three relentlessly physical electronic sets can become exhausting when there is nowhere for the intensity to dissipate. At Łącznik, it could. The outside conversations, pauses and meetings with the bands gave the evening breathing space, while every return indoors felt like deliberately re-entering the pressure. Three approaches, one increasingly crowded dancefloor What I liked most was that the evening had progression without needing an artificial concept imposed on it afterwards. Antibody made the body move through rhythmic precision and rave-derived momentum. Agonoize turned the same physical response into confrontation, participation and grotesque theatre. System Noire then took an audience already pushed far beyond passive listening and drove that energy through the dynamics of a full, forceful live set. The crowd grew thicker, sweatier and considerably bloodier as the night progressed, but the atmosphere never became hostile. Quite the opposite. There was a great deal of warmth underneath the noise: people dancing, talking outside, meeting musicians, returning inside and throwing themselves back into it. And perhaps that is the detail worth keeping. With music this aggressive, the obvious vocabulary is always brutality, darkness, violence and impact. All of those things were present. What made the Wrocław show successful, however, was how much pleasure there was inside that aggression. Antibody looked playful behind the pounding rhythms and wandering frogs. Agonoize turned theatrical bloodshed into something the front rows actively wanted to share. System Noire finished with smoke, light and enough accumulated movement to make the floor feel barely contained. By the end, Klub Łącznik looked appropriately wrecked, and the people inside it looked extremely happy. About Agonoize, System Noire and Antibody Agonoize formed in Berlin in 2002 around vocalist Chris L. and have built more than two decades of work around harsh electronic music paired with extreme, theatrically violent stage shows. Their most recent full studio album, “Revelation Six Six Sick,” was released through RepoRecords in April 2021; Side-Line marked that release with a streaming concert announcement at the time. Earlier releases include the 2019 EP “Blutgruppe Jesus (-) / Schmerzpervers 2.0” and the album “Midget Vampire Porn.” Ahead of the Wrocław date, Side-Line interviewed Chris L. about returning to the stage after a serious illness and new material. System Noire, from Hanover, were founded in 2016 and marked their tenth anniversary in 2026. Side-Line first profiled the project in a 2017 Face The Beat feature. The band’s sound has expanded from its original electronic base to include guitars and a heavier industrial-metal edge, documented on the 2024 album “Aftermath” and the February 2025 single “Lost Control.” Antibody is the project of Jan Laustroer, who began releasing music under the name in 2013 at the age of twelve. Side-Line introduced Antibody in a 2016 Face The Beat profile and later featured the track “Secrets” as a 2019 free download. Laustroer’s debut album, “Opera of Death,” followed in 2017, with “Never Quite Right” arriving in 2024. In January 2026, Antibody collaborated with Grendel on “The Ranidae.” Agonoize, System Noire and Antibody played Klub Łącznik, the concert venue inside the Czasoprzestrzeń cultural centre at Wrocław’s former Dąbie tram depot, on September 25, 2026.

items.body: John Coltrane – The John Coltrane Quartet Plays (Impulse, 1965) By Dan Sorrells Most of my listening hours are spent on freely improvised music. But when it comes to Coltrane, I love the classic quartet, 1965, right before things broke open (and the group, apart). The John Coltrane Quartet Plays is what I reach for most often. “Chim Chim Cheree” starts like another “My Favorite Things,” but less than a minute in, Coltrane’s already chafing against the melody, and after two he and Jones are fairly bursting out of Tyner’s measured vamp. “Brazilia” and “Nature Boy” enticingly point toward the searching explorations to come, where ideas were turned inside-out in dizzying, kaleidoscopic epics (something further evidenced by various surfaced recordings from the Half Note during the same period, where “Chim” and “Song of Praise” stretch to twice the length). The sense that traditional song forms must still be made to contain Trane’s increasingly frenetic probing lends indelible tension to the music; these songs are like swelling water ballons, but they’re filled with boiling water. For those of us in the future, it’s all the more heightened when you know just how far things will get pushed, even before the close of the year. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: It’s been quite a number of years since I read the Dune series, Frank Herbert’s legendary sci-fi epic depicting the struggle to control the eponymous desert planet and its space travel-enabling spice, but a recent discovery has made me want to read it again. That discovery is April Larson’s album “You Stand in a Valley Between Dunes”, a work conceived as a tribute to the power and imagination of the Dune universe. Louisiana-based Larson has quite an extensive discography up on Bandcamp, including both her own ambient work and her collaborations with Matt Bower as the duo Isobel Ccircle~, but it was her Dune-themed collection that initially caught my ear. The album displays a preference for classic warm ambient music, but this is classic warm ambient done right: big, expansive chords, gradual changes, simple harmonic progressions, and buried details are here in abundance. Low fluttering rumbles are often used to convey the impression of galaxy-crossing speed onto weighty drones that otherwise shift quite slowly; on the couple of occasions where conventional beats are used, the effect is one of steady progression or even stasis. In ‘Brimstone and Cinnamon (Selim Wormrider)’, a muffled beat and piano-like broken chords are gradually overtaken by a general rumbling and insistent thump (perhaps as the giant worm burrows into the sand). Meanwhile, pieces such as ‘The Hubris of Josef Venport’ and ‘Glittering Flakes of a Shredded Cosmos (A Vision of Leto II)’ use a more ambiguous approach to harmony to create a mysterious, even mystical impression. Most of the 14 tracks on “You Stand in a Valley” are quite short; some end before I’ve had chance to fully immerse myself in them. But what the album excels at is in drawing out the dialectic common to the desert, to space, and to ambient music: that is, the perception of huge vastness and great intimacy in the same moment. I remember the early days of home digital music production and the huge glut of sci-fi-themed music that could be found on the nascent Internet; how it felt as if the future was accelerating towards us at ever-faster speeds. Now it’s possible to listen to such music in a nostalgic mode, as just another ‘retro’ genre dredged up from the past in order to hide a general stagnation and lack of ideas in the present. By way of contrast, “You Stand in a Valley Between Dunes” encourages the listener to imagine a future big enough to encompass the stars, and as close as the grains of sand in your hand. You Stand in a Valley Between Dunes by April Larson April Larson
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是对弗兰克·赫伯特科幻史诗《沙丘》宇宙的致敬之作。April Larson以经典温暖氛围音乐手法构建：宽广扩展的音色、渐进的和声演变、低频轰鸣的嗡鸣，营造出沙海与星际旅行的感官印象。专辑14首曲目大多偏短，部分尚未完全沉浸便已结束，但整体擅长捕捉沙漠、太空与氛围音乐三者共同的辩证张力——在同一瞬间呈现浩瀚辽阔与亲密细腻的并存感。曲目中既有沉稳鼓点与钢琴碎和弦被吞没于隆隆低频的画面，也有以模糊和声营造神秘甚至神秘主义氛围的作品。专辑鼓励听者想象一个能容纳星辰的未来，并感受手中沙粒般的近切质感，以氛围声响回应了早期数字音乐时代对未来的憧憬。

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: Alison Cotton 的新专辑延续了她一贯的模糊美学，将民谣、前卫音乐与宗教仪式感融为一体。专辑以中提琴、管风琴、击弦古钢琴和钢琴为核心乐器，并加入鼓、贝斯与合成器扩展音色层次。多数曲目为即兴录制，一次性完成，营造出穿越时空的低语氛围。她将英国自然诗人 John Clare 的诗句谱入《I Am!》，用持续的低音嗡鸣托起超脱的旋律；《Sprigs of Heather》从中世纪圣咏式开场发展为钢琴主导的缓降乐思，被视为全专辑的珍珠之作。这张作品同时是一份纪念，献给 2024 年底去世的父亲，《The Final Harvest》以静穆方式记录了他最后一次造访心爱菜园的时刻，光与暗在音轨间彼此渗透，情绪不断流转。整张专辑拒绝被简单归类，既是 Cotton 风格本身的延伸，也跨越了流派与时代的界限。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由瑞典小提琴家与挪威父子乐手组成三重奏，对斯堪的纳维亚传统舞曲素材进行非传统的重新诠释。乐评指出，作品虽源自舞曲旋律，但呈现出室内乐般的质感——三位演奏者沉浸在亲密的音乐对话中，探索旋律中隐藏的意义与暗流。音乐人各自背景跨越民俗、跨界实验与现代作曲领域，演奏中刻意模糊流派边界，时而使用柔音管、萨克斯、风笛等非常规乐器编配。编曲手法上，旋律层与即兴质感伴奏相互交织，结构时有瓦解与停顿，呈现出碎片化的解构美学。这种对北欧民间素材的实验性再创作，融合了传统与现代、即兴与室内乐的多元特质。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家Omar Sosa的专辑《Sendas》录制于意大利Fazioli音乐厅，基于两小时的独奏即兴录音，后混入稀疏的人声采样、打击乐、循环音和实地录音。Sosa受Thelonious Monk启发，追求每次演奏的不可重复性，风格跨越爵士、拉丁、古典却刻意回避类型标签。专辑强调冥想式创作，将钢琴内部琴弦的共振与电子音效融合，探索低脉轮共鸣的声音理念。Sosa反对流媒体算法对音乐的分类逻辑，坚持首遍录音的自然性，以'少即是多'为信条，制作上保留即兴的原始精神再施以后期调味。

items.body: In his latest guide to the best new music coming out of France, David McKenna considers the relationship between regionalism and nationalism, and reviews essential new records, from a mutant club masterpiece to a brilliant prog pop swansong, via Sourdure, Brama and more Brama Last year, Anna Mahtani’s Organic Intelligence newsletter for tQ subscribers provided an excellent primer for the music that has accompanied the revival of Occitan, the Romance language that was once spoken throughout southwestern France and parts of Italy, Spain and Morocco. It was also extremely timely, as 2026 is proving to be a vintage year for Occitan music. items._cn_summary: 这篇乐评聚焦于法国近期发行的音乐作品，探讨了地方性与民族主义之间的关系。核心话题围绕奥克语（Occitan）音乐的复兴展开，奥克语是一种曾经通行于法国西南部及意大利、西班牙、摩洛哥部分地区的罗曼语。文章提及了Cocanha的《Flame Foclòre》以及Sourdure、Brama等多位音乐人的新作，涉及从突变俱乐部（mutant club）杰作到前卫流行（prog pop）绝唱等多种风格。乐评将这些作品置于语言复兴与地域文化身份认同的语境中审视，强调奥克语音乐在2026年呈现出的丰收态势。整体内容偏向于区域性世界音乐传统的当代演绎，融合了电子实验元素。

And yet Cooked is as finely balanced as a champagne cascade. The beauty of Cooked is in this balance. Each musical... The post Oren Ambarchi – Cooked appeared first on The Quietus.
items._cn_summary: 奥伦·阿姆巴尔奇的新专辑《Cooked》历时三年录制，横跨三大洲五个国家，邀请十三位音乐人参与，使用了尺八、口哨、便携管风琴以及爵士领域的多种乐器。两首长篇作品展现了精妙的平衡感——尽管参与人数众多、乐器繁杂，整体却如香槟瀑布般层次分明。最引人注目的是高度处理的人声元素的加入，为以器乐即兴和音色探索为核心的专辑增添了出人意料的维度。这张作品延续了阿姆巴尔奇在实验音乐领域一贯的探索路径，将极简音色延展、即兴结构与多元文化乐器编织在一起，既具冒险精神又不失结构控制力。

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Third album in three years after taking 18 years to create their first one, Architecture might sound/read like a logical successor to their previous one, but there is quite a sonic progression here;eve,n if SS' collective paws are plainly recognizable. Indeed, we've taken a steep turn away from Avant-Prog, but I"m not sure this is due to the new arrival Katie's saxophone on three tracks, because it doesn't really change the overall soundscapes, even if the energy reach a different level and intensity - for the better, I might add. But indeed, the general sonic direction of this album tells us that we are at a corner of the band's career.The dissonance element present in their first two albums has almost disappeared, and this helps the accessibility o�f their music. Relatively absent from their first two album, there is a sense of drama permeating most of the tracks, endearing us to their musical escapes and extravaganzas. Emotional melodies over tight rhythms. BTW, it was their first album directly sold in CD, and for both formats, SS took the carte to make an attractive sleeve with a transparent protecting plastic sleeve. TBH, I really don't know why the band will change its name and record label (I guess the departure of their violinist played a big role), after the release of their best-yet album . But there will be two undeniable links: the Architecture link (purposely misspelled) and the same type of line-up (new violinist) and a now-permanent sax player replacing the too-discreet guitarist. but that's for their next album. In the meantime, their third is definitely the one I preferred at the time.
items._cn_summary: 这是乐队三年内推出的第三张专辑，在保持原有辨识度的同时展现出明显的声学进化。整体风格从前作的前卫激进路线转向更易接受的方向，不协和元素大幅减少，旋律性与戏剧性显著增强。评论指出萨克斯的加入并未从根本上改变音景结构，但提升了能量与强度。情绪化旋律与紧密节奏的结合成为新专辑的核心特征，这也是评论者认为乐队最佳作品的原因。专辑在编排上展现出从前卫摇滚向室内乐气质过渡的倾向，情绪张力贯穿始终，但创新幅度相对有限，更多是乐队原有语言的打磨与延伸，而非根本性的突破。

items.body: Ductape Faded Flowers Swiss Dark Nights Turkish duo Ductape have been gathering a following on the basis of a steady stream of singles and albums, in a very of the moment sound. More than anything, the duo of Çağla Güleray and Furkan Güleray have found a style that sits between the gloomy darkwave of She Past Away and the more light fast-moving quirky post-punk that we’ve come to associate with Molchat Doma and their ilk, with a touch of modern electro-darkwave for taste. And while their latest LP Faded Flowers is certainly very au courant in terms of the songwriting and performances, there’s also no denying that the band have a talent for it. Listening to cuts like “Figures” or “Gölgesiz” should give a good idea of Ductape at their most straightforward; there’s a strong propulsive bassline backed by stiff kicks and gated snares, plenty of tremelo’d guitar lines and the charismatic vocals of Güleray, who imbues her low moans and whoas with plenty of muscle. It’s a sound the band never stray too far from, but keep fairly fluid, adding in some synth leads (as on the zippy “Delilik”) or touches of other styles (the italo-infused intro of “Burn”) to taste. And while the record does have a certain sameyness to it, it’s fast-moving and has enough switch-ups to keep things moving, such as placing the occasional combo-breaker like the oompah-cabaret stylings of “Velvet Dawn” into the middle of the album. That said, the band’s bag of tricks has its limits, and multiple listens will show some of their weaker tendencies. A big one would be their general production sensibility: the bass and guitar sounds don’t vary much, their drum programming leans on eighties drum machine toms for fills to the point of distraction, and Güleray, for her confidence and power always sits in the same place in the mix, always up front, never varying in dynamics or range. To that point, these songs are often short of an actually memorable hook, usually relying on simple repeated keyboard licks or a simple refrain to fill the role. The fact is that even on multiple listens songs will tend to melt into one another, with only a few really standing out by virtue of having a vastly different tempo or arrangement. “Sad Gravity” is perhaps the most interesting song simply by virtue of using some more fully-fleshed out electronics and touches of spanish guitar. You can see why folks would enjoy a record like Faded Flowers, it’s got a sound with proven appeal, performed expertly and with enough verve to wallpaper its musical shortcomings. Having it on is never unpleasant, and it’ll no doubt have folks dancing at your local goth club, but there’s simply not enough substance here to rise above perfectly fine. Ductape are a band that probably have a really good record in them, and it’ll be interesting to see how they get there from here. Buy it. Faded Flowers by Ductape The post Ductape, “Faded Flowers” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: Ductape 是一支来自瑞士的土耳其双人组合，新专辑《Faded Flowers》延续了他们近年流行的暗潮/后朋克风格，介于 She Past Away 的阴郁与 Molchat Doma 式的明快冷感之间。贝斯线条强劲推进，鼓机与嗵鼓音色贯穿始终，吉他与合成器旋律交替出现，女主唱 Çağla Güleray 的低吟充满力量。歌曲结构紧凑、节奏明快，部分曲目融入意大利迪斯科元素或西班牙吉他点缀。乐评肯定了乐队的演奏功底与声音吸引力，但也指出制作音色变化有限、旋律钩子不够突出、歌曲易趋同等问题。整体而言，这是一张完成度不错、适合暗潮俱乐部场景的专辑，但在声音深度与突破性上仍有提升空间。

items.body: Tiiva This Could Be A Start UK producer's soundtrack to an imaginary video game delivers a maximalist hyper pop sucker punch blue fifty-nine/this could be a start by Tiiva Video game design and hyperpop share a clear sonic DNA, defined by maximalism, shape-shifting identities and non-linear structures. From the music genre’s inception, its most formative artists have embedded game tropes into their digital soundscapes. With This Could Be A Start, Lake District-based producer and game designer Tiiva delivers a compelling addition to this well-trodden collision of spaces. The result is a euphoric, emotionally resonant record, despite occasional forays into over-reverence toward the pop pioneers it draws from. Released on cassette under the catalogue number blue fifty-nine, the record finds a home on UK label Blue... The post Tiiva – This Could Be A Start appeared first on The Quietus.
items._cn_summary: 英国湖区制作人Tiiva以游戏设计师身份发行了这张卡带专辑，将电子游戏音效设计与hyperpop美学相融合。专辑试图构建一个虚拟电子游戏的配乐空间，运用最大化编曲策略和碎片化结构，与游戏设计领域的多重身份转换和非线性叙事共享声音基因。评论指出作品在情感共鸣方面表现突出，但也存在过度致敬hyperpop前辈的问题，缺乏足够的原创突破。整体制作在声音设计和情绪张力上有一定水准，但更接近既有类型框架内的延伸，而非开创性实验。发行于英国独立小厂牌Blue Fifty-Nine，以卡带为载体呈现出特定的复古数字美学倾向。

items.body: In August of this year, New Focus Recordings released New Music for Two Voices, an impressive collection of acapella vocal music by sopranos Susan Narucki and Kirsten Ashley Wiest. This lavish album features a full hour masterful singing of six contemporary works, including three world premiere recordings. Susan Narucki is an accomplished soprano who has appeared as a soloist with the Cleveland Orchestra, Los Angeles Philharmonic, the San Francisco Symphony, among many other international appearances. She is presently on the faculty of the Department of Music at UC San Diego. Kirsten Ashley Wiest is an award-winning coloratura soprano who has performed and recorded alongside numerous GRAMMY winners, the Los Angeles Philharmonic, San Diego Symphony, Bang on a Can All-Stars and the Partch ensemble, among many others. Kirsten currently teaches voice at San Bernardino Valley College and University of California Riverside, New Music for Two Voices is a deep dive into the cutting edge of virtuoso vocal technique as it intersects with contemporary musical composition. The album is accompanied by excellent liner notes, full translations of the texts and biographical notes on the composers and the performers. The outstanding sound engineering is by Andrew Munsey and Kristina Tran. The first track on the album is come sempre (2025), by Dutch composer Rozalie Hirs. Although written just last year, the liner notes inform that this piece “…evokes music of an earlier time, with shifting tonal centers and interwoven melodic lines..” Running at over 7 minutes, it is one of the longer works of the entire album and is a world premiere. come sempre features two voices singing separately in Italian, sometimes together and sometimes in a call and response pattern. The vocal lines are often independent and weave in and around each other seamlessly in a series of lovely harmonies. There is no accompaniment anywhere in this album so the two singers must rely on their internal sense of rhythm and pitch. Where crisp phrases are present, these are always clean and punchy. Nothing ragged or blurry here; the notes are precise and balanced. As the piece proceeds it gradually increases in complexity, summoning ever greater technique. The singing by these two confident voices, however, is always controlled throughout. The poems of El trino persistente by Javier Tafur González are the inspiration for TRINOS, a series of twelve miniature works by Colombian composer Alba Potes. Commissioned by Susan Narucki in 2024, all are less than one minute long, yet these pieces sparkle like brilliant gems. The liner notes state that “Each of the twelve settings seems to capture a moment in time—by turns, lyrical, nostalgic, jubilant, hopeful.” “TRINOS: I. Jazmin” is the first of the twelve pieces and although less than a minute in length, it sets the standard for the precision and vocal technique that is heard throughout the entire work. A high vocal tone opens, then falls rapidly in pitch as a second voice joins in a middle register with dissonance. The singers must rely on their own intuition for pitch and timing – there are no accompanying chords or common rhythms. The overall feeling is one of welcome and portent. Although less than a minute in length, this first piece sets a high bar for vocal artistry. Other pieces in the work are similarly concise and illustrate the consistent level of virtuosity brought to bear by Wiest and Narucki. “TRINOS: II. Entra illuminando la casa”, at just 32 seconds in length ,is intense, with many jumps and leaps in the two voices. It shines like a fiery jewel. “TRINOS: IV. No saldré” features a middle register voice together with a lower voice in close harmony. Stretches of unusual dissonances challenge the singers, but are navigated successfully. “TRINOS: VI. Timida flor” opens with a strong voice soaring up very high with impressive power and good control. “TRINOS: VII. Ven, anclemos” is soft, with almost mournful feeling and quietly sentimental. The text, even in English translation, is perfect: “Come, let us anchor now hands entwined.” “TRINOS: IX. Se hundió el buque” by contrast, is completely different. A quiet, solo voice is heard in a middle register, reserved and subdued. The lyrics are more spoken than sung, producing a purposeful and deliberate sensibility. “TRINOS: XI. Podemos estar juntos” is another solo piece with a strong voice crying out as if in sadness. The singing here is expressive, yet delivered with great clarity. The final piece in the work is “TRINOS: XII. En los hilos”, a duet with the lower voice in sustained tones underneath a soaring, coloratura voice. The dissonances in the harmonies add a powerful, melancholy feeling to this. TRINOS is a masterful collection of small pieces that each deliver an emotional punch from the virtuosity of the performers. The third work on the album is From the Grammar of Dreams (1988), by Kaija Saariaho and consists of five pieces based on two separate texts from the American poet Sylvia Plath. The liner notes tell us that “The five duets demonstrate Saariaho’s unique compositional language, with its attention to fine gradations of vocal color, intricacy and flexibility of gesture, and a nearly overwhelming range of emotional expression.” The first duet, labeled simply “I”, opens with strange and painful sounds in the lower voice with struggling vocals in the second voice as if forcing out the words and notes. Leaps and jumps are heard in the upper voice accompanied by sustained and plaintive sounds from the lower. Just a little over 2 minutes long, this piece is expressively weird and haunting.“II”, the second piece in From the Grammar of Dreams begins with two sets of spoken words heard simultaneously. This is somewhat chaotic as there is no common tones or phrasing. One voice includes some rather gruesome details, as if recounting a nightmare. The voices are alternately speaking and singing and often very agitated. The music is complex and dynamic, yet confidently delivered. The third duet, “III” is soft and melodic; completely different in character from the previous pieces. There is lovely harmony in the two voices with lots of sustained notes and dramatic gestures. There is a welcome and mysterious feeling to this. “IV” opens with scratchy, breathy sounds followed by strong vocal music. The voices jump and soar as each part bounces breathlessly off the other. The two voices devolve in a sort of shouting match just before the piece concludes with a few short breaths. Amazing technique here. The final duet, “V”, begins with a series of sustained notes in both voices sung in a high register with prominent vibrato. The sounds loop around each other independently in pitch and dynamic. This produces an eerie feeling at times but is mostly strongly declarative. The fourth work on the album is NauðaR Níu [The Nine Needs] (2025), by Jeffrey Holmes. This collection of nine pieces is based on old Norse Runic carvings (ca. 5th through 12th century), as compiled and translated by the composer. As with the other works in this album, each piece is short, ranging from 37 seconds to a little over three and a half minutes. As explained in the liner notes, NauðaR Níu features some unusual accompaniment: “Throughout, the vocalists play a variety of percussion instruments; the sound of metal, skin, wood and natural materials contributing to the sense of a vast primeval landscape.” The opening piece of NauðaR Níu, titled simply “I”, starts with soft tones by two voices. As this one minute piece proceeds, a gentle gong sound and some light percussion are heard; a subtle and mysterious beginning. “II” sets a completely different tone. A sharp drum rap begins, serving as a starting exclamation point. The two voices weave in and around each other in sustained tones amid much howling and spooky vocals. Another series of bangs from the drum and a woodblock add to the unnerving atmosphere. “III” returns to a more settled and soothing feeling. A low sustained vocal in one voice is made more expressive by the light tinkling of chimes. Very mystical and solemn with lovely vocals and reverential sentiment. “IV” continues in a sacred feeling, opening with an Ahhh sound in a single voice. Another voice joins in, accompanied by quiet gong tones and a low drone. The exotic – almost Asian – feel of this is supported by devout vocals, gentle chimes and percussion. “V” continues in the exotic groove and returns to the more forward style with drum raps and sharp woodblock beats. The voices seeming to chant with out words but in eerie, sustained tones. There is a decidedly spectral and anxious feeling to this. “VI” returns to the more subdued refinement heard in “IV”, with a soft opening and chimes. A sudden drum strike with wood block recalls the mood in “II”. A gong is heard between the sustained and almost mournful vocals. There is a sacred, worshipful feel to this. “VII” continues with chimes and a high, plaintive opening vocal. The top voice soars in very high, airy sweeps. More chimes accompany. The excellent singing, heard in very high registers, is controlled, on pitch and does not lose its power. “VIII” opens with a strong drum strike and woodblock rap. Loud, almost screaming vocals are heard, as if in great surprise. A palpable sense of danger and fear is present. Loud drum and woodblock strikes accompanied by long, descending sweeps of vocals paint a convincing musical portrait of fear and despair, This sets the stage for the final section, “IX” which opens with a haunting vocal solo , soon joined by the second voice in call and response. The voices are subdued with somber descending pitches and accompanied by drum strikes, chimes and gong strikes. All elements of the various sections seemingly combine into a sense of acceptance and fateful resignation. Beautiful, expressive singing is heard as the vocals fade to the finish. With NauðaR Níu, Jeffrey Holmes has forged a vibrant musical connection between the Old Norse culture and our own.The next work on the album is a collection of five short pieces titled Two Walking (1994) by French composer Pascal Dusapin. The text for Two Walking is by American writer Gertrude Stein and the work was originally conceived by Dusapin as a study for his chamber opera To Be Sung. The opening piece of Dusapin’s collection, titled “I. How many little wings” begins with a single lyrical voice followed closely be a second vocal, almost as an echo. Now the higher voice soars in a sustained upward arc with text following in both voices. The vocals bounce and dance around each other, evoking birdlike acrobatics on the wing. As the tempo increases the text becomes louder and more frenetic. A sudden slowing towards the finish provides the listener with a soft landing. “ II. Kiss my lips” begins with a quiet clicking and two voices in a sort of conversation. There is a whispering and intimate feel to this, sung as if in secret. “III. May, June” opens with a long solo note followed by the second voice entering slightly below in a counter melody. Now the notes in each voice volley back and forth effectively. As the text moves faster, crisply sung in short, quick phrases, the result is a pleasingly complex texture that does not sacrifice the beautiful harmonies. “IV. A scene in singing” has both voices starting together but soon singing separate lines. Short snappy phrases are heard in places and at times the harmony is unusual, but the overall effect is both lovely and abstract. The final piece in the Dusapin work is “ V. It seems to be”. Two voices in lower register open in syncopated rhythms and the separate vocal lines produce an engaging, crunchy texture. The pitches and harmony are controlled and balanced, even with the lively phrasing. “ V. It seems to be” is a fine finish to an intriguing work. The concluding work on the album is Melisande (2022), by Marti Epstein, the longest piece at almost 13 minutes. Inspired by the Debussy opera, Epstein re-imagines the story as if told through Melisande’s own experience, rather than as a reflection of others. In this interpretation, “the two sopranos alternate between extending and finishing each other’s words, functioning as a single unit, or singing passages with overlapping, contrapuntal lines that give way to moments of ecstatic release.” Melisande opens with two sustained voices in a delicate harmony and dynamics that vary intriguingly. The vocals become more active, with independent lines weaving in and around each other in a call and response pattern. By 4:10 the voices are singing in common phrases in an effective contrast to the opening. The upper voice is especially impressive, exhibiting a fine tone with strength and confidence. By 7:10 the vocals are in solid harmony and declarative text sung expressively in middle registers. The lines diverge and become occasionally independent, one often following the other. The duet singing here is especially disciplined and precise. At a slowing of the tempo, Melisande fades quietly to its finish. An excellent performance of technically challenging music.New Music for Two Voices is a dazzling exploration of vocal virtuosity that sets – and meets – a very high standard. Hopefully this premiere album by Susan Narucki and Kirsten Ashley Wiest will be the first of more to follow. items.excerpt: Just when Steve Reich’s ninetieth birthday celebrations appeared to be drifting towards an inauspicious conclusion, along comes Charles Hazlewood and the Paraorchestra to gatecrash the party, tear up the rulebook, let loose a posse of Dionysian dancers on the scene, and transform a routine Reich event into a Bacchanalian rave. items.body: Just when Steve Reich’s ninetieth birthday celebrations appeared to be drifting towards an inauspicious conclusion, along comes Charles Hazlewood and the Paraorchestra to gatecrash the party, tear up the rulebook, let loose a posse of Dionysian dancers on the scene, and transform a routine Reich event into a Bacchanalian rave. This new take on Music for 18 Musicians provided a breath of fresh air amongst a raft of retrospective events—Reich remodelled and refracted through the prism of psychedelia and 1990s warehouse EDM, with perhaps a whiff of hippy idealism and transcendental meditation thrown in. I’m not sure whether the composer would have approved. Most of those present gleefully lapped it all up. Hazlewood is known for thinking creatively outside the box, but here he appeared to be operating according to a completely different set of Euclidean principles. To be sure, Reich’s music has been placed in a variety of unorthodox settings and spaces over the years, ranging from disused train station buildings and repurposed multistorey car parks to all manner of outdoor locations, so there was nothing inherently radical in presenting this classic work at Southbank Centre’s Clore Ballroom. Nevertheless, dotting the ensemble around the space went against Reich’s own recommended set-up, as did Hazlewood’s encouragement for everyone to move about the space as if viewing an audible sculpture in an art gallery. Likewise, the idea of dancers moving in and around the ensemble was not in itself revolutionary. Reich’s music, including Music for 18, has provided accompaniment to several dance productions in the past, notably those of Laura Dean Dancers and Musicians, and Anne Teresa De Keersmaeker’s Rosas dance company. However, the idea of interpolating freestyle, improvised movement seemed to fly in the face of the piece’s austerely conceptual pretext. Hazlewood rightly drew attention, in a brief announcement at the beginning of the evening, to a whole range of paradoxes that lie at the heart of Reich’s music—not least that between rigor and freedom—and it was certainly refreshing to see Music for 18 unfettered from its structuralist straitjacket. There’s certainly nothing wrong with shaking things up, so long as the intention is motivated by creative and artistic concerns rather than dramatic effect. While there’s no doubting that Hazlewood’s intentions were genuine, the results were not always persuasive. The dance element, pre-planned beforehand, tended to shift attention from the sonic experience to a visual one, and while the idea of encouraging the audience to move in and around the space was in keeping with Music for 18’s ‘immersive’ impact, this too became something of a distraction. Many members of the audience appeared to circumambulate the space in a kind of somnambulistic daze, and the whole point of the exercise—to listen more attentively to the music—seemed to go by the wayside. I can’t imagine for a moment that walking around while trying to avoid bumping into other people doing the same thing might in any way sharpen one’s focus on the complex layers and textures that underpin Reich’s groundbreaking work. Thankfully, most seemed to have had enough of moving around after the opening set of eleven pulsing chords. So much for walking as a gradual process. I remained firmly anchored to the vibraphone station—the composition’s ‘signal box’ and timekeeper—where the rest of the ensemble could be heard in more-or-less perfect balance. What seemed to get lost in all the theatrical paraphernalia was the music itself, which was a shame since the Paraorchestra’s performance was never less than impressive, and at times quite brilliant. Highlights included brightly hued, bell-like clarinet and vocal buildups in Sections II, IV and IX; surging tonic-dominant movement in the pianos in Section IIIa; warmly glowing and flowing marimba and vocal colours halfway through Section V; and excellent ensemble coordination in Section X. And despite my cautious reservations about the happening-style multimedia nature of the performance, Sections VI–VIII, with their infectious maracas groove, yielded an extraordinarily uplifting synergy between music, dance and movement. At that moment, the entire performance clicked into place. As an experiment, this presentation of Music for 18 certainly possesses potential, but perhaps it’s worth taking a closer look at those early, gritty, grungy performances of minimalist music in New York’s large lofts and gallery spaces during the late 1960s and early ’70s. Photos of these early performances show audiences scattered about the venue, as was the case here, but sitting (or lying down) on cushions rather than walking around, with an amplified ensemble positioned at the centre of the room. Perhaps future audiences should be encouraged instead to bring a beanbag, lie back, and let the music wash over them, wave after beautiful wave… The post Steve Reich at 90: ‘Music for 18 Musicians’ (The Clore Ballroom, Southbank Centre, London, 27 September 2026) appeared first on Sequenza21.

items._cn_summary: 为庆祝Steve Reich九十岁生日，指挥Charles Hazlewood与Paraorchestra重新演绎了《Music for 18 Musicians》。演出将作曲家严谨的极简主义结构与自由即兴舞蹈、迷幻电子氛围以及仓库锐舞能量相融合，打破了原作的固定舞台布局，让演奏者散布于空间各处，观众可自由走动体验。乐评指出，Reich音乐本身曾多次与舞蹈合作，但此次融入自由即兴动作的尝试与作品的极简概念形成张力。视觉元素的介入虽然活跃了气氛，却也分散了听众对声音本身的专注力，削弱了原作的冥想特质。整体而言，这是一次大胆但效果不完全令人信服的实验性重构，在打破结构主义束缚与保持原作听觉纯粹性之间未能找到完美平衡。

items.body: Hey friends, quick update from the Senior Staff on the eve of the spooky season. It’s been real busy for us in both in non-IDUD related life stuff, and as such it’s very possible we are overlooking new records and artists that we should have our eye on. Thus it’s time for a renewal of our annual plea to please, tell us what we haven’t covered that you think would be to our taste. You can do it right here in the comments of this very post? As much as we enjoy a good dig through Bandcamp and various setlists from respected DJs and friends, we’d love a blindspot check from our readers, who have generally never steered us wrong with that sort of thing. We’d sure appreciate it. Seven Trees Mesh, “Trying to Save You” Bristol’s Mesh are such a unique quantity in the big umbrella that is Our Thing. Taking synthpop and rendering them with rock band energy isn’t the easiest move in music, but they’ve always pulled it off with aplomb. See new single “Trying to Save You” from the forthcoming mini-album “Fallen Angel” for example; big hooks, bold arrangement choices (that switch up as it exits the chorus is so clever) and lots of momentum. Truly no other band sounds like them. Fallen Angel by Mesh Aurat, “XIII” Coming just a few months after the dense and spiky Cobra EP, this teaser from Aurat’s forthcoming silhouette LP portends something quite different from the highly touted and fast moving LA act. Forsaking their EBM tendencies, this cut carries their goth/post-punk genome into unexpected doomgaze territory. Is it reflective of the whole release? We’ll be sure to follow up in a month’s time. silhouette by Aurat Kontravoid, “Chances” Kontravoid is no stranger to writing a great electro-pop jam; you could probably build a decent mixtape out of cuts from across the catalogue like “Too Deep”, “Losing Game” and “Faceless”. Strong possibility you’d throw “Chances”, another taste of the upcoming Sound of the Void to that list also, it’s exactly the kind of catchy, danceable, melancholic but forceful cut that Cam Findlay has been casually knocking out for some time now. We wouldn’t be shocked to hear this at any given goth club or darkwave party over the next couple of years, it’s fun and spooky in the right ways. Sound of the Void by Kontravoid Chalice Sect, “Silent Fever” Chalice Sect is a new name to us but it doesn’t take long to cotton onto the LA act’s rhythmically pummelling read on darkwave on this track from their forthcoming Finis Initii EP. A slew of heavily distorted synths which sound as though they have more in common with the aggro side of synthwave than goth drives things further into a maximalist space which will likely irritate purists but probably goes off live quite well. Finis Initii by Chalice Sect Nasdrowie, “Impact” Shout-out to friend Nick for bringing this EP from Nadrowie to our attention. It’s largely instrumental, but the vocals on “Impact” position it as the sort of murky 90s electro industrial that is like candy to us. Raw and rough, you could hear this being spun in a set with any number of classic Zoth bands. For fans of Evil’s Toy, and maybe Seven Trees? A New World To Cry by Nasdrowie Seven Trees, “Underneath My Skin” Speak of the devil, here’s a pleasantly moody and stark new cut from the aforementioned reactivated Swedish dark electro vets Seven Trees. As with their 2021 comeback LP Dead/End “Underneath My Skin” isn’t trying to leap off the page at you, but as the simple but solid structure beneath the clean and icy programming rolls along, the track progressively builds a sense of dread and inevitability that leaves a lasting chill. Solid and considered stuff for those who prioritize mood and affect in their dark electro. Underneath My Skin by Seven Trees The post Tracks: September 27th, 2026 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: Cold night, middle of winter Bodies in motion, flames burning high Now I wake up alone, the air doesn’t move No rain on the concrete, no god in the sky Soft Vein’s Another Summer walks into the long-held mythology of summer breeziness with a raised eyebrow and a very good synthesizer. Justin Chamberlain treats the season less as paradise than as evidence: proof that time keeps circling back while the people inside it become harder to recognize. The title carries its own little cruelty. Another chance, another repetition, another invitation to believe that whatever went wrong might somehow correct itself on the next pass. Chamberlain sounds far too experienced to buy the brochure. His interest lies in the distance between recurrence and recovery, and in the uncomfortable realization that repetition rarely restores what has already changed. Soft Vein has been pushing further into new wave and synthpop this year, and Another Summer may be Chamberlain’s sharpest turn in that direction yet. There is plenty of mid-’80s Peter Gabriel and Robert Palmer in its bloodstream, especially in the combination of clipped electronic percussion, broad keyboards, soulful vocal phrasing, and a hook built with enough confidence to survive outside the black-clad electronic underground. Chamberlain has found a sweet spot between pop polish and emotional frostbite. The bass is wonderfully round and physical, moving beneath the track with the lazy certainty of something expensive rolling down an empty boulevard. Keyboards spread outward in great glassy planes while Chamberlain’s emotive voice occupies the center with an appealing mixture of restraint, desire, and resignation. He sings like a man who has learned that romantic memory becomes increasingly unreliable the more often you consult it. Cameron Noel Dunbar filmed the video during a visit to Soft Vein’s rehearsal studio a couple of weeks ago, capturing Chamberlain and his live band preparing for their upcoming shows. The footage offers an intimate portrait of the musicians together before heading out on the road, preserving the shared concentration and easy familiarity of rehearsal. Dunbar layers the rehearsal footage with psychedelic superimpositions, letting faces double, equipment drift through bodies, and colors smear across gestures. The room gradually starts behaving like memory itself: imperfect, cumulative, prone to placing several moments on top of each other. That treatment suits a song preoccupied with desire and repetition, while the footage preserves something more immediate: the pleasure of being in a room together, preparing to bring these songs to an audience. Watch the video for Another Summer below: Mixed by Chamberlain and mastered by Jason Corbett of ACTORS at Jacknife Sound, Another Summer appears on Soft Vein’s album All We’ve Known of Heaven, out now through Artoffact Records. CD and vinyl preorders are available now through Bandcamp. Listen to Another Summer below and order All We’ve Known Of Heaven here. items.body: Belgian electronic pop project 808 Dot Pop, the solo outlet of Passenger S of Metroland, will release two companion studio albums, “Minimalism” and “Maximalism,” on November 30, 2026 through Alfa Matrix. Both are available for pre-order now on CD and as digital albums, and together carry 18 tracks based on a concept drawn from 20th-century architecture. A three-track digital single, “minimalism EP,” preceded the announcement on September 25, 2026, serving as a lead-in to both records. ‘Minimalism’ and ‘Maximalism’: two companion albums, one concept “Minimalism” is described by the label as the “white album” and “Maximalism” as its “black album” counterpart. Passenger S spent time studying architectural literature, essays and video material after being “ignited by Habitat 67,” and composed both albums around forms and atmospheres tied to specific buildings and architectural movements. “Every sound, left or right stereo effect, was chosen with intent, allowing space, repetition, and restraint to play an important role alongside melody and rhythm,” the label states. The project takes listeners through architectural landmarks in Spain, Canada, Japan, Germany, the UK, France and Australia. Recommend to fans of Kraftwerk, Komputer and Orbital. Formats and pricing for ‘Minimalism’ and ‘Maximalism’ Both albums are available as a CD, priced at €11.99 each through the Alfa Matrix store, with release confirmed for November 30, 2026. Both are also available as digital albums on Bandcamp, as “Minimalism” and “Maximalism”. ‘Minimalism’ tracklist “Minimalism” runs nine tracks, each named after an architectural “ism” paired with the building that inspired it: “rationalism (palazzo terragni)” “minimalism (glass house)” “bowelism (centre pompidou)” “contextualism (fallingwater)” “modernism (villa savoye)” “facadism (mitsui honkan)” “parametricism (kunsthaus graz)” “brutalism (habitat 67)” “internationalism (van nelle fabriek)” Minimalism by 808 DOT POP ‘Maximalism’ tracklist “Maximalism” also runs nine tracks, following the same naming pattern: “purism (lovell health house)” “cubism (kovarovicova villa)” “ecoism (heliotrope)” “structuralism (cube houses)” “neofuturism (guillemins)” “expressionism (einsteinturm)” “maximalism (waldspirale)” “formalism (opera house)” “deconstructivism (museo guggenheim)” Maximalism by 808 DOT POP The ‘minimalism EP’ lead single Ahead of the full albums, 808 Dot Pop released “minimalism EP” on September 25, 2026, as a digital-only three-track release on Bandcamp. Its tracklist: “minimalism (farnsworth house)” (2:58), “contextualism (at&t long lines)” (3:31) and “minimalism (koshino house)” (5:47). The EP’s description calls it “a dialogue between rhythm and space, merging electronic grooves with analogue sequences that loop with subtle, human variation,” inspired specifically by the Farnsworth House, the AT&T Long Lines Building and the Koshino House. Side-Line previously covered the video series accompanying the campaign, which set individual tracks against the Seagram Building, Habitat 67 and Fallingwater, and noted plans for a “Foundationalism” bonus EP on an NFC-equipped card and a 72-page companion book titled “Essentialism,” both announced as fan-shop exclusives ahead of the album release. minimalism EP by 808 DOT POP About 808 Dot Pop 808 Dot Pop is the solo electronic pop project of Sven Lauwers, known as Passenger S, a member of the Belgian synth-pop duo Metroland. He launched 808 Dot Pop as a way to work outside “the Metroland bubble,” describing the project at its debut as lighter and more playful than Metroland, leaning toward a Düsseldorf-influenced techno-pop sound that uses warm analogue sequences, melodic synthetic layers and the Roland TR-808 drum machine that gives the project its name. 808 Dot Pop’s debut album, “The Colour Temperature,” arrived in 2020 on Alfa Matrix, preceded by the singles “Blackbodies – pulsation,” “Blackbodies – variation” and “Jingle Pop.” The same year brought a run of additional singles and a limited 7-inch vinyl release. In 2022, the project marked Bandcamp Friday with four singles released at once. In March 2023, 808 Dot Pop returned with a larger release cycle built around a “Pop Radio” concept, naming the albums and EPs after broadcast frequencies: the CD-only albums “FM88.2” and “AM1350,” the download-only “MW720,” and the EPs “FM101.4” and “AM685.” Passenger S has said the idea began after he asked permission from OMD’s Andy McCluskey to cover the track “Radio Waves,” and grew from there into a wider exploration of radio history reaching back to Guglielmo Marconi’s early crystal-radio experiments. The two CD albums were built as continuous “broadcast” listening experiences, with guest vocals from Lis van den Akker and a co-writing credit for Gary Hunter of Kraftman. 808 Dot Pop followed with a double EP in June 2023. The project’s back catalogue has also been reworked by fellow Alfa Matrix act Cubic, who released the 808 Dot Pop rework album “Back To 808” in December 2025, followed by the twin EPs “CB-708” and “CB-128” in February 2026, revisiting the same source material. “Minimalism” and “Maximalism,” due November 30, 2026, mark 808 Dot Pop’s next studio albums since the 2023 “Pop Radio” releases, again pairing companion releases with a shared concept, following the same working method Passenger S has applied to the project since its debut.
items._cn_summary: 比利时电子流行项目808 Dot Pop将以建筑学概念为核心，发行双胞胎专辑《Minimalism》与《Maximalism》，共收录18首作品。创作灵感源自20世纪建筑文献，Habitat 67激发了整体构思，每首曲目以建筑流派命名并对应特定建筑，如玻璃屋、蓬皮杜中心、Habitat 67等。制作理念强调空间感、重复与克制，左右声道效果经过精心设计，将旋律节奏与建筑氛围融为一体。专辑由独立厂牌Alfa Matrix发行，CD售价11.99欧元，已开放预购。此前已发布三首数字单曲EP作为预热。推荐给Kraftwerk、Komputer和Orbital风格的爱好者。整体概念富有结构性与主题性，但在声音创新层面尚待实际聆听验证。

items.body: 040118180514 and 102119200914. No, these aren't the result of my cat stepping on my keyboard; they're pseudonyms for the members of Endspace, an experimental black metal duet hailing from Canada, who have been constantly reinforcing their "sci-fi black metal" sound through a trail of releases leading up to their debut record—or "transmission", per the record's pattern of naming each song as a sequential broadcast. Whatever is contained within First Contact, it's going to be alien as hell. As predicted, First Contact is hypnotizingly strange. Dissonant metal genres are already on another plane of disorientation, but Endspace ramp the perplexity up tenfold, via the myriad synths, electronics, and vocoders at the duo's disposal, mostly implemented in their "singing". 040... and 120...'s vocals genuinely sound like extraterrestrial communications. After thirty-nine minutes however, the gimmick gets tiring. In fact, the second transmission alone exemplifies how overpowering their incomprehensible "vocals" can be. Across the nine transmissions, the "vocals" range from the pitch of a dog whistle to murky, gurgly depths, and once—during "Seventh Transmission"—can you pick up a robot warning the "system engaged." Everything, including that excerpt, is also always too loud for whatever mood First Contact is currently in, with zero instrumental tracks providing a much-desired break. "Ninth Transmission", is a particular offender, being constructed in a repeating calm/harsh pattern, and the recurring blasts have a high chance of blowing an eardrum or two.It sucks, because underneath the alien mess that are the vocals, Endspace play commendable dissonant and technical black metal. The streak from the "Seventh" to "Ninth" transmissions, plus the chug-centered niceness that is "Third Transmission", all feature guitar-forward, chaotic deliciousness, whose overhaul of electronics donates a symphonic feel to the record. This helps the otherworldly atmospheres, with the positively overpowering climax of "Fourth Transmission" providing the pinnacle of symphonics. Elsewhere, keyboard lines sound like opera notes and any synth undertone majorly assists any song it's found in. The tracks without a metal attitude, however, leave room for the aforementioned annoyances that are the vocals. The "Second", "Fifth", and "Sixth" transmissions are the definite weak spots in First Contact, with the fifth leaning too much into a noisy electronic beat.While the execution of First Contact was as experimental and wacky as I hoped it'd be, I bit off way more than I could chew with this LP. Tinny, vocoded emanations bury rather pleasing metal, resulting in a listen that I'm not anticipating returning to anytime soon, and doesn't further my desire for Endspace to make a second acquaintance. items.body:
A debut, digital-only EP from a Danish trio, led by one of the Nordic folk scene�s outstanding and experienced vocalists, Mia Guldhammer. Five tracks, with the musicians bringing their own perspectives to mostly traditional music. There�s a lovely ancient, creaky mood throughout.
The opener, �Svennedal,� with its rough, cantering rhythm, offers a perfect shop window for Guldhammer�s impressive, persuasive voice, while jaw harp and bagpipes bring an insistent propulsion to �Nordg�rd,� the only original here, by band member Morten Musicus.
Cimbalom adds a delicate backdrop to the traditional �Agnete Of Bjergmanden,� with Guldhammer�s soft jaw harp offering extra textures to the other instruments, as it brings a springy opening to the final cut, �Orms�,� mingling with flute and strings to create something quite thrilling and off kilter on this instrumental.
Five tracks, and an introduction to a band that already seems very mature and accomplished. A strong beginning � what will GuldGanger do with an entire album?

items.body: Review by brainsuccasurgery — *Limite Acque Sicure* by *Limite Acque Sicure*?a surprising title and surname, a sort of metaphor with multiple possible levels of meaning: the cartographic contours of the Mediterranean Sea in the Middle Ages? A body of water of a certain depth, not to be exceeded? The knowledge of our inner selves (or that of others), beyond which it may be dangerous to venture? The need to push past our own limits in order to grow? Or simply the name of a red wine from Abruzzo? Please refer to the very interesting lyrics on this album for a hint of an answer (be sure to have an Italian translation tool on hand if you don't speak the language). Musically speaking, you don't need to be an expert on Banco's music to understand that *Limite Acque Sicure*, hailing from Ferrara and formed in 2005 by singer Andrea Chendi and keyboardist Antonello Giovannelli as just one of many tribute bands, is a true devotee of the golden age of the Nocenzi brothers' band?a fact confirmed by the inclusion on this self-titled album of the iconic "Il Giardino Del Mago" (Banco 1972), in a dazzling live version.Between the introductory "Sogno D'Oriente" (12:48)?with its oriental sounds, as its name suggests, reminiscent of the famous "Kashmir"?and the short "Ti Salver� " (2:11)?placed at the other end, in the style and spirit of Banco's "Traccia II" (that album again) Certain tracks on *Limite Acque Sicure* stand out more. These are the ones where the band most clearly demonstrates that it has something personal to convey to us. "Terra Straniera" (7:53), with its majestic, enthusiastic, and determined finale, is closer in style to *Prowlers* than to *Banco*; "Il Respiro Dell'Anima" (8:25), with its more lively rhythm, ambitious structure, and shimmering arrangements that leave plenty of room for highly effective guitar and Moog solos. And above all, the epic "Fiamme Intorno " (10:48), with a darker main theme (though carried by a deceptively light rhythm), as if weighed down by a relentless exploration of humanity's spiritual wanderings, then giving way to a second, more open and luminous section, full of hope, whose coda?and this is quite unexpected?features a few drum beats dedicated to? Neil Peart. On a more contemporary note, the music of Limite Acque Sicure evokes memories of Museo Rosenbach, Campo Di Marte, Il Rovescio Della Medaglia, Alphataurus, and Apoteosi, all those meteor-like bands that shone for the duration of a single album (often released in 1973) before disappearing for a long time?or forever. "Limite Acque Sicure" seems to be a tribute to the RPI of the past, yet one that looks toward the future. In other words, it is less a relic of a glorious past than a promise of what the RPI may have in store.

items.body: Review by Warthur — Bakerloo's sole album reveals them as a truly diverse progressive group of the early prog era. They've clearly emerged from the same blues rock primordial soup formented by the Yardbirds and Bluesbreakers and Cream and which saw peers like Jetbro Tull and Black Sabbath emerge. Bakerloo actually shared a manager with Sabbath, but it's Tull who you'll be reminded of most - in particular, the sound of their earliest days, before Mick Abrahams left. There's no flute, but plenty of harmonica - and the power trip work in enough influences from jazz and classical music to suggest a group just as broad in influences as Tull, though perhaps with more influence from the calmer, more meditative side of psychedelia creeping in at points.It's no surprise that they fell by the wayside at the end - this was a crowded scene, after all, and it was all too easy for groups to get lost in the shuffle, and with Tull already evolving away from their early blues influences and Black Sabbath turning the blues into doom metal their peers were moving to distinguish themselves, so you can see why Bakerloo were in danger of being eclipsed. In retrospect, it's a gem of its particular scene - it's just that the scene in question was on the cusp of being overtaken by other strands of prog and blues-derived rock.
